articles.title: Despite a WA law meant to help, the DOE keeps fighting Hanford workers' comp claims
articles.author: Lizz Giordano
paras: Lonnie Rouse shuffled into a wood-paneled conference room at the Washington state Capitol in March 2018. It had been nearly a decade since medical experts diagnosed him with a neurological disease they attributed to his exposure to chemicals at work. In the time since, he had acquired a stutter, begun limping and lost several teeth biting into a banana.

For nearly 20 years, Rouse had packaged plutonium and monitored radioactive waste at the Hanford Site , a now-decommissioned Department of Energy nuclear weapons production plant in south-central Washington and one of the most contaminated nuclear sites in the country. Tanks full of radioactive sludge exposed him to at least 48 potentially hazardous chemicals . The worksite was so toxic, he said, that the floor once melted the rubber off his boots.

Rouse was among the thousands of workers responsible for the ongoing environmental cleanup at Hanford, which has been underway since the DOE shut down the last reactor in the late 1980s. Congress has acknowledged , based on voluminous studies, that radiation at DOE sites poses health risks to workers.

Over time, some people at Hanford became so sick they could no longer work. Like Rouse, they filed for workers’ compensation. The DOE consistently challenged their claims and tried to shift the blame onto the workers themselves.

By the time Rouse took his place behind then-Gov. Jay Inslee, he was desperate. His 2009 workers’ compensation claim had been denied. He had burned through his retirement savings and declared bankruptcy.
As he watched, the governor signed a bill that was supposed to change his life.

For years, Hanford employees filing workers’ compensation claims had to prove the chemicals they were exposed to on the job made them sick. The new law Inslee signed flipped that burden of proof. Under the law , agencies were instructed to presume that working at Hanford had caused certain cancers, neurological diseases and respiratory illnesses . Now the Department of Energy would have to prove to the state that something other than the job had made the workers sick if it wanted to deny their claims.

Rouse thought the presumption law would speed up his claim for benefits. State lawmakers and the former governor thought it would force the DOE to take responsibility for the harm Hanford workers were experiencing.

But despite the law, the DOE continues to fight new and existing claims, Cascade PBS and ProPublica found. We asked the state for claims records going back to the presumption law’s passage in 2018, but the state only provided records going back three and a half years, to 2023. In that period, workers filed 102 new claims for benefits, state data shows. The DOE did not recommend approving a single one.
The state, which has final say, overruled the DOE and approved 75% of those claims. The DOE appealed all but seven of those approvals.

Cascade PBS and ProPublica spoke to workers, surviving family members, lawyers representing workers and state officials. They all pointed to a pattern: The DOE systematically challenges and then drags out workers’ compensation claims for years with recommended denials and subsequent legal appeals. Along the way, it has spent millions on outside lawyers and expert testimony, including doctor evaluations that point to other causes for workers’ illnesses.

The DOE has paid out benefits to Hanford workers in some cases, lawyers and families said, but it has done so while still actively appealing the claims. It warns workers that they may have to pay the money back.

Our reporting found that not even death ends the cycle of appeals. About 152 workers’ claims remain stranded in this legal limbo — approved by the state but still under appeal by the DOE. Half of those workers are dead. The DOE continues to fight to deny their families survivors’ benefits.

“It seems pretty coldhearted, calculated, that they’re trying to save money on the back of sick workers who they made sick,” said Gerry Pollet, one of the Washington state representatives who sponsored the 2018 presumption law, who is also a co-founder of the Hanford cleanup watchdog group Heart of America Northwest. “That’s why we needed a state law.”

After Cascade PBS and ProPublica raised questions about the DOE’s pattern of litigating claims, regulators at the Washington State Department of Labor and Industries met twice with DOE staff, state agency spokesperson Carrie McCausland said. But she could not point to any other actions the agency has taken beyond the two meetings.
“Agency staff are concerned and are right now assessing the severity of patterns we’ve seen,” McCausland wrote in an email.

The DOE did not answer detailed questions or respond to the newsrooms’ findings. In a statement, a spokesperson wrote that the DOE is following “all applicable local, state, and federal laws” and “has a long and successful record of accomplishment of protecting human health and the environment.”

The DOE has the right to file multiple appeals against a claim. According to court records, its appeals have sought to overturn claims approved by the state, narrow the period of back wages, or block survivors’ benefits, among other things. In appeals filings, the DOE’s lawyers have argued that factors other than work at Hanford played a role in the workers’ illnesses, including smoking, drinking, obesity or genetics.

In Rouse’s case, the energy department blamed alcoholism and family conflicts. The state agency that handles appeals did not find those arguments persuasive. DOE awarded Rouse most of his back pay in 2024, his lawyer said. Rouse declined to say how much that was, but said he is not touching the money until the legal process concludes.
In the nearly eight years it has been fighting his claim, the DOE has filed more than 20 appeals contesting different aspects of his claim.

“We were always told that nothing is out here that's going to harm you — you do what you are supposed to do, and you do what you are trained to do, and you're going to be fine,” said Rouse, who now receives 24-hour care.

The smell of ammonia serves as a warning, workers say, that the underground tanks holding a mix of radioactive sludge have burped chemical vapors into the air above. From 1998 to 2008, it was Rouse’s job to monitor the toxic waste held in the “tank farms.” The containers together hold more than 50 million gallons of liquid waste. Rouse says he lost count of how many times tanks released toxic vapor that took his breath away, sometimes knocking him to the ground and making him vomit and bleed from his nose. According to a 2014 report funded by the federal government, tank farm workers exposed to chemical vapors commonly reported nausea, headaches and nosebleeds.

The liquid sloshing around in those tanks represented the radioactive byproducts of the Cold War. Hanford produced two-thirds of the plutonium for the nation's nuclear arsenal and fueled the atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki, Japan, in 1945.

The end of production in the late 1980s launched a cleanup effort that is expected to continue until at least 2086. As of January 2025, more than 13,000 people were working at Hanford, nearly all of them for private companies contracted by the DOE. It is one of the largest and most expensive efforts to remediate toxic waste in the nation’s history.

In 2000, Congress passed the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act , which provides medical care and one-time payouts to workers at DOE sites across the country. It was an acknowledgement that the nation’s nuclear weapons workers had been exposed to radioactive substances known to cause cancer. In it, lawmakers referred to a DOE policy “to litigate occupational illness claims, which has deterred workers from filing workers’ compensation claims and has imposed major financial burdens for such employees who have sought compensation.”
But the benefits of the federal program were limited: It capped payouts at $400,000.

Washington's workers’ compensation system, by contrast, can provide steady wage replacement or a pension benefit, in some cases, for the rest of an injured employee’s life. It’s a program that can easily surpass the maximum federal benefit.

The state went further with its 2018 presumption law. Such laws generally protect firefighters who are regularly exposed to smoke, burned plastics and extreme heat. The National Council on Compensation Insurance, the Washington state attorney general and Pollet all said they were unaware of any other state that has extended that protection for radiological workers.
The federal government challenged Washington’s state law later that year in court, arguing it was discriminatory because it only applied to Hanford and the DOE.

Anticipating a Supreme Court decision that ultimately agreed, lawmakers passed an expanded version that covered all workers at “radiological hazardous waste facilities” in the state, including the state’s only functioning nuclear power plant and a French-owned facility that manufactures nuclear fuel rods. Nonetheless, roughly 75% of the 428 claims filed since 2018 have come from the DOE’s Hanford workers, according to the state Department of Labor and Industries.

Kathleen Kersey spent 10 years at Hanford, during both the production and cleanup stages. Much of her work involved measuring radiation around the site and making sure levels were safe. She says her safety training covered radiation, but not other hazards like chemical vapors burping from the waste tanks.

Kersey struggles to walk, has short-term memory problems and at one point lost vision in her right eye for three months. A doctor diagnosed her with multiple sclerosis, which is a neurological disorder, one of the categories of illnesses the state’s presumption law recognizes as related to chemical exposure at Hanford. In 2019 she filed a claim, which the state approved.
The DOE has appealed, arguing that something other than her time at Hanford caused her multiple sclerosis.
Kersey is one of the 152 workers still awaiting a resolution on her workers’ compensation claim. The DOE has not paid her any back wages, she said. The DOE declined to comment on her case.
“I feel depleted and disgusted,” Kersey said of the appeals process. “It makes me feel like I'm worthless. I have no value.”

State records show that the DOE has filed more than 500 appeals since the presumption law passed in 2018. In 20 cases, as it did with Rouse, the DOE has appealed a single worker’s claim half a dozen times or more.
“We have seen tremendous pushback from DOE on essentially almost every single case that's been brought,” said Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown.

Rouse’s wife, Melinda, said she knew something was wrong when he could not remember how to cut an orange. His vision started to blur, he stumbled often, and suddenly he felt irritable all the time. His primary care physician first thought he might have had a brain tumor. The physician referred him to a neurologist who noted cognitive impairment, possibly due to exposure to multiple toxins at the Hanford Site. The neurologist then referred him to a neuropsychologist, who diagnosed him with “toxic encephalopathy” in 2009, saying it was “more likely than not” that chemical exposure damaged his brain, according to court records.

The U.S. Department of Labor agreed too, approving him in 2010 for benefits under the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act, saying it was “at least as likely as not” that Hanford contributed to his illness. A federal medical consultant even praised the neuropsychologist who assessed Rouse for his “unusually thorough analysis of causation.”
Rouse refiled his 2009 state workers’ compensation claim under the new law in 2018. Washington state approved it later that year.

If you liked Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G the first time around, you’ll like this less; if you disliked it, you’ll dislike this more; if you suspected it was racist, you’ll be more emboldened to say so – especially as Baron Cohen has dreamed up a whole new character apparently to pre-empt and mock precisely that objection. Broad and crass as it often is – in fact always is – this Ali G sequel is sometimes funny: the athletic vigour of our hero’s pranking and punking is like the umpteenth Jackass film at which you might find yourself laughing, and Baron Cohen blunders with the semi-intentional force of an XL bully into the issue of whether jokes are still allowed.

Unlike the first film, Ali G in Da House from 2002, this is not a full written-through narrative. It is basically another live-ammo series of hoaxes with some spectacular bad taste perpetrated upon the deserving and less deserving; it satirises the shamelessness of anti-woke free speech martyrs, punching up and down with grossout cringe, and the targets include some big names who shouldn’t be revealed here. There are two other subordinate characters: Erran Morad, a sinister Mossad/IDF officer turned US security consultant (who appeared in Baron Cohen’s Who Is America? TV series ), and a new figure: Dr Nira Cain-N’Degrocello, a grotesquely supercilious white liberal who is the self-appointed scourge of cultural appropriation. According to a 2014 report funded by the federal government, tank farm workers exposed to chemical vapors commonly reported nausea, headaches and nosebleeds.

The liquid sloshing around in those tanks represented the radioactive byproducts of the Cold War. Hanford produced two-thirds of the plutonium for the nation’s nuclear arsenal and fueled the atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki, Japan, in 1945.

The end of production in the late 1980s launched a cleanup effort that is expected to continue until at least 2086. As of January 2025, more than 13,000 people were working at Hanford, nearly all of them for private companies contracted by the DOE. It is one of the largest and most expensive efforts to remediate toxic waste in the nation’s history.

In 2000, Congress passed the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act , which provides medical care and one-time payouts to workers at DOE sites across the country. It was an acknowledgement that the nation’s nuclear weapons workers had been exposed to radioactive substances known to cause cancer. In it, lawmakers referred to a DOE policy “to litigate occupational illness claims, which has deterred workers from filing workers’ compensation claims and has imposed major financial burdens for such employees who have sought compensation.”
But the benefits of the federal program were limited: It capped payouts at $400,000.

Washington’s workers’ compensation system, by contrast, can provide steady wage replacement or a pension benefit, in some cases, for the rest of an injured employee’s life. It’s a program that can easily surpass the maximum federal benefit.

The state went further with its 2018 presumption law. Such laws generally protect firefighters who are regularly exposed to smoke, burned plastics and extreme heat. The National Council on Compensation Insurance, the Washington state attorney general and Pollet all said they were unaware of any other state that has extended that protection for radiological workers.
The federal government challenged Washington’s state law later that year in court, arguing it was discriminatory because it only applied to Hanford and the DOE.

Anticipating a Supreme Court decision that ultimately agreed, lawmakers passed an expanded version that covered all workers at “radiological hazardous waste facilities” in the state, including the state’s only functioning nuclear power plant and a French-owned facility that manufactures nuclear fuel rods. Nonetheless, roughly 75% of the 428 claims filed since 2018 have come from the DOE’s Hanford workers, according to the state Department of Labor and Industries.

Kathleen Kersey spent 10 years at Hanford, during both the production and cleanup stages. Much of her work involved measuring radiation around the site and making sure levels were safe. She says her safety training covered radiation, but not other hazards like chemical vapors burping from the waste tanks.

Kersey struggles to walk, has short-term memory problems and at one point lost vision in her right eye for three months. A doctor diagnosed her with multiple sclerosis, which is a neurological disorder, one of the categories of illnesses the state’s presumption law recognizes as related to chemical exposure at Hanford. In 2019 she filed a claim, which the state approved.
The DOE has appealed, arguing that something other than her time at Hanford caused her multiple sclerosis.
Kersey is one of the 152 workers still awaiting a resolution on her workers’ compensation claim. The DOE has not paid her any back wages, she said. The DOE declined to comment on her case.
“I feel depleted and disgusted,” Kersey said of the appeals process. “It makes me feel like I’m worthless. I have no value.”

State records show that the DOE has filed more than 500 appeals since the presumption law passed in 2018. In 20 cases, as it did with Rouse, the DOE has appealed a single worker’s claim half a dozen times or more.
“We have seen tremendous pushback from DOE on essentially almost every single case that’s been brought,” said Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown.

Rouse’s wife, Melinda, said she knew something was wrong when he could not remember how to cut an orange. His vision started to blur, he stumbled often, and suddenly he felt irritable all the time. His primary care physician first thought he might have had a brain tumor. The physician referred him to a neurologist who noted cognitive impairment, possibly due to exposure to multiple toxins at the Hanford Site. The neurologist then referred him to a neuropsychologist, who diagnosed him with “toxic encephalopathy” in 2009, saying it was “more likely than not” that chemical exposure damaged his brain, according to court records.

The U.S. Department of Labor agreed too, approving him in 2010 for benefits under the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act, saying it was “at least as likely as not” that Hanford contributed to his illness. A federal medical consultant even praised the neuropsychologist who assessed Rouse for his “unusually thorough analysis of causation.”
Rouse refiled his 2009 state workers’ compensation claim under the new law in 2018. Washington state approved it later that year.

articles.title: Surviving cancer starts at diagnosis and continues after treatment – earlier survivorship care can help patients feel better and live longer
articles.author:
<name>Marci Lee Nilsen, Professor of Otolaryngology, University of Pittsburgh</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/marci-lee-nilsen-2770476"/>
paras: “You have cancer.” It’s a phrase that comes as a shock, then is quickly followed by a whirlwind of decisions that somehow feel fast and slow at the same time.

You have treatments to decide on. You are trying to figure out how you might work, care for your family and undergo a variety of intensive medical appointments all at the same time. You are centered on the here and now, and thinking about five or 10 years down the road is not at the forefront of your mind. Getting through treatment is the finish line you are reaching for; that is when you may actually feel like a cancer survivor.

As a nurse and scientist who has spent over a decade caring for cancer patients and studying ways to ease the effects of treatment, I have heard this story time and time again from both survivors and their loved ones. But survivorship actually begins at the time of diagnosis.

In fact, in our newly published research in JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery, my team and I found that patients with head and neck cancer who started survivorship care – healthcare services that support a cancer survivor’s physical, emotional, social and practical needs – earlier were more likely to stick to treatment and be alive without cancer three years after treatment.

Clinicians and researchers consider a person a cancer survivor from the time they are diagnosed through the end of their life. More important than the term is what cancer survivorship is meant to look like for the patient.

Cancer survivorship reflects the patient’s experience with cancer and cancer treatment, and the physical, emotional and social effects that has on their life. Survivorship care is designed to identify and address the complex needs of a cancer survivor beyond just the physical changes. It involves coordinating care and promoting the person’s overall health and well-being.

This care can look different for each patient, depending on the cancer they have and their individual needs. For example, my team and I designed a survivorship clinic at UPMC in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to address the most common issues head and neck cancer survivors experience. In addition to surgeons and nurses, our team includes swallowing therapists, a physical therapist, a dental care team and a dietitian to help address issues with swallowing, nutrition, dental health, physical function and mood. All of these services are offered at the same location and can be completed in one visit on the same day, generally under one copay.

After the visit, the cancer survivor, their oncology team and their primary care clinician receive a care plan to help coordinate care and communication among all their providers. Rather than as a one-time session, our survivorship clinic builds relationships with survivors, supporting them as their needs change over time.

While a person becomes a survivor at the time of diagnosis, most survivorship care is delivered after the initial treatment has ended. This may be partly because to be accredited by a major medical body that sets cancer care standards, the American College of Surgeons Commission on Cancer , hospitals must offer at least three services to cancer survivors after they complete their initial treatment.
While survivorship care can ease physical and psychological issues after cancer treatment, survivors often report significant unmet needs before and during treatment.

In my specialty of head and neck cancers, many patients undergo a grueling five to seven weeks of radiation therapy, often in addition to chemotherapy. They experience a host of side effects: pain, mouth sores, skin burns, difficulty swallowing and weight loss, which together can lead to treatment interruption and hospitalization . These side effects often continue and sometimes worsen years after treatment .

While our survivorship clinic was initially designed for patients who completed treatment, we later expanded our services to patients before radiation. We previously found that starting survivorship care before radiation was associated with better quality of life and reduced symptoms .

In our newly published research, we found that among 471 cancer survivors, 62% of those who attended our survivorship clinic before completing radiation finished treatment on time , compared with 48% of those who were not seen before completing radiation. At three years, 60% of patients seen in the survivorship clinic before completing radiation were alive and cancer-free, compared with 39% of those not seen before completion. The association remained after accounting for whether patients completed radiation on time, suggesting that on-time completion may not fully explain the difference.

Although our results suggest that shifting the start of survivorship care to before treatment may improve outcomes, they do not prove it. Our team plans to test in a larger clinical trial whether starting survivorship care before radiation helps patients finish treatment on time and maintain quality of life, while also examining how teams coordinate care and referrals.

Comprehensive cancer care implies not only a comprehensive treatment plan, but also supportive care that will help patients live well beyond their diagnosis and treatment. However, a 2024 survey of 384 facilities accredited by the American College of Surgeons Commission on Cancer found that only 1 in 5 programs estimated that most of their eligible patients receive survivorship care .

For head and neck cancer survivors specifically, nearly all clinicians routinely assess cancer recurrence, swallowing and thyroid function. But only about half address psychological symptoms , such as anxiety and depression, and fewer than 1 in 3 addressed body image or sleep problems.

Survivorship care is often framed as care that begins after treatment ends, which can delay patients’ access to support during treatment. Communication breakdowns may leave patients unaware of available services, while a lack of referrals can keep them from receiving needed care. Survivorship care also draws on clinicians with different areas of expertise, and some hospitals and treatment centers may lack enough dedicated staff time to provide a full range of services.
The end of treatment is a huge milestone that patients and their loved ones reach for. But it is not where survivorship care truly starts.

Making survivorship care more accessible may help make cancer care more comprehensive. Clinicians and researchers can start planning for the survivor’s life after cancer even when it’s not on the patient’s mind. Bringing a team that combines treatment experts with rehabilitation and supportive care specialists into the room early can help achieve better outcomes for patients.
As a cancer survivor or a loved one, you don’t need to wait.

Marci Lee Nilsen receives funding from the National Institutes of Health and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation. She directs the UPMC Head and Neck Cancer Survivorship Clinic, which was the setting for the research described in this article.

articles.title: Indian Gen Z ‘cockroach’ protesters aim to upend assumptions about democracy – and populism – in Modi’s India
articles.author:
<name>Amrita Basu, Professor of Political Science, and Sexuality, Women's and Gender Studies, Amherst College</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/amrita-basu-802879"/>
paras: Five months after its founding , India’s Cockroach Janta Party, known as the CJP, has revealed what youth-led democratic movements can achieve – and how hard they are to sustain.

The movement was formed in May 2026 to protest the government’s cancellation of medical school entrance exams and after India’s Chief Justice Surya Kant likened unemployed youth to cockroaches. By July, the largely Gen Z movement had scored an early victory with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The CJP has since moved on to a much larger political issue: critics’ claims that the Election Commission has deleted approximately 130 million names from the voter rolls. Since Oct. 2, protesters have descended on the streets of Delhi, Mumbai and other cities demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, halting the deletions pending an independent inquiry, and the restoration of the old electoral rolls before the next elections.

In the process, the CJP has encountered strong government resistance. . Amid a crackdown on protests, two of the movement’s spokespersons – Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das – were detained , while Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his right-wing populist Bharatiya Janata Party have refused to bend on the voter roll issue – instead accusing protesters of undermining democracy.

Nonetheless, as a long-time scholar of Indian political parties and social movements , I believe the CJP’s protests have revealed people’s deep-seated anxieties over democratic erosion in a country of nearly 1.5 billion. Through courage and acerbic wit, the CJP has done something that has eluded conventional opposition parties over the past 12 years: puncturing the ruling party’s aura of invulnerability . In doing so, I believe the protests have challenged the government’s view of who “the people” are, what democracy means, and who speaks for youth, women and the politically marginalized.

Modi often describes India as the “Mother of Democracy,” a reference to its civilizational heritage and to Bharat Mata, the Hindu mother goddess. Democracy, he insists, is not a Western import but a native inheritance. The implication is meant to be reassuring: Modern India has always been democratic and always will be.

But some outside monitors disagree. Sweden’s V-Dem Institute classifies India as an “ electoral autocracy ,” meaning that although it regularly holds multiparty elections, it fails basic democratic benchmarks such as legislative and judicial checks and balances and citizens’ active political participation.
Judged by how the country treats dissent, the record is damning: using anti-terrorism laws to jail activists without trial , barricading protest sites, internet blackouts and police brutality .

By contrast, the CJP considers peaceful protest, along with upholding the country’s constitution, essential elements of democracy. Demonstrators regularly circulate images of B. R. Ambedkar – the chief architect of the Indian constitution – on posters, in slogans and in songs. Like Ambedkar, 30-year-old CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke is a Dalit, or untouchable within the Hindu caste system.

Critics argue that the Bharatiya Janata Party defines the nation through Hindu civilizational identity , which is exclusionary because it rejects India’s rich Muslim historical traditions and casts doubt on the political loyalties of the country’s Muslims, who constitute about 14% of the population – 197 million people. By contrast, the CJP draws no line between insider and outsider by faith, caste or birth, and it defines community by shared commitments.

The voter roll struggle shows what is at stake in the question. The Election Commission says the revision will remove duplicate entries, deceased voters and noncitizens . But critics worry that the burden of proof falls on voters. Consider how hard it is for poor Muslims, Dalits and migrant workers to produce decades-old birth, education and land certificates. Moreover, those whose names are struck from the electoral rolls fear being branded illegal immigrants .
While the Bharatiya Janata Party had held the prime minister’s office before, Modi’s 2014 election marked a sea change in Indian politics, disrupting the Congress Party’s dominance.

The BJP owed it electoral success in part to attracting young and first-time voters with promises of employment, economic growth and what is known in Hindi as “ achhe din aane waale hain ,” or “good days are coming.” Since the BJP took office in 2014, the country has charted strong GDP growth, but the macroeconomic success has been belied by ongoing and rampant inequality that falls especially hard on the poor and young.

The BJP claims to have fulfilled some of its more targeted campaign promises, such as engaging in merit-based public sector hiring . Yet 40% of Indian college graduates under 25 are unemployed . Paradoxically, the unemployment rate for youth who cannot read and write hovers around just 3.4%. For college graduates, who are the Cockroach Janta Party’s main constituency, it is nearly nine times higher at roughly 29% .

Seizing on this building discontent, the CJP uses the slogan “Achhe Din” ironically, on posters and memes. Its manifesto opens: “If you are going to call us cockroaches, the least you can do is pay our rent.” It calls for making “lazy” – a code word for the unemployed – a protected political identity.

Underlying the joke is a serious point: that stigmatization of the jobless offends millions of impoverished people, something critics note is protected in the dignity and equality guarantees of articles 21 and 14 of the Constitution.

The Bharatiya Janata Party has gained women’s electoral support through a combination of targeted welfare schemes, support for increased women’s representation in legislatures and endless talk of women’s empowerment, or “nari shakti .”
However, masses of women protesters have challenged state-defined women’s empowerment. They stop police vans carrying detainees, scale barricades and criticize the prime minister.

One of the most prominent among them is Neha Bora, a Ph.D. student and president of the left-wing All India Students’ Association, whose blunt messages to Modi has seen her profile skyrocket. Modi has said he has been subject to vulgar abuses by the protesters and was shocked by how “our daughters” could use such foul language, but he viewed them as “misdirected children” and was ready to forgive them .

The throngs of women who are protesting express deep discontent with the government’s paternalism. They challenge its Hindu-inflected understanding of empowerment and insist on speaking for themselves rather than being spoken for. They express outrage at the government’s brutal response to their peaceful protests. They describe how the police have beaten and sexually harassed them, while anonymous self-styled guardians of religious morality engage in doxing, threats of rape and acid attacks, and circulate demeaning AI-generated images of them. For protesters, that record sits uneasily besides the prime minister’s denunciation of violence against women .

The CJP motto, “Cockroaches never die,” has wide resonance. Protesters have survived, but not escaped, violence, incarceration, internet blackouts and police blockades. The sunglass-wearing cockroach mascot makes a mockery of leader-centered nationalist branding.

Recent youth-led uprisings in Bangladesh and Nepal have shown how quickly online mobilization can outrun official control. What distinguishes the CJP is that it pairs humor with legal and technical infrastructure. Its online portal Saakshi vault , which means “witness,” collects photos and videos of police violence that protesters upload; volunteer lawyers use these to issue complaints against officers.

The CJP’s recent and remarkable successes do not mean that the movement is likely to disrupt the BJP’s hold on power in the next parliamentary elections in 2029. For now at least, the CJP is fairly concentrated in urban strongholds and would need to build organizational infrastructure and develop long-term demands.

However, a generation that a government minister wrote off as lazy and expendable has exposed the cracks in the system that the chief justice defended. Whatever form it takes, the movement provides a vision and reminder of what democracy looks like.

Amrita Basu has received research funding from the Social Science Research Council, the American Institute of Indian Studies, the Ford Foundation, the John D. and Catherine T. McArthur Foundation, and Amherst College.

articles.title: Tech Moves: 2 Microsoft execs depart; Kymeta hires former CIA leader; Alaska Air names CITO
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: — Kymeta has appointed former CIA Deputy Director Elizabeth Kimber as chief growth officer.

Kymeta, a Redmond, Wash.-based mobile satellite communications company, is working to increase sales with the Department of Defense, the intelligence community and other organizations in national security.

Kimber had a 37-year career with the CIA, departing in 2022 as the agency’s deputy director for operations. She most recently worked as a vice president with Two Six Technologies and has served on Kymeta’s board of directors for two years.

— Alaska Airlines has named Amaresh Siva as its first chief information technology officer. Siva joins from CVS Health and has held technology leadership roles for more than two decades at companies including Lowe’s, Target and GE Money.

“Technology touches nearly every part of how we run our airline and serve our guests, and Amaresh will bring our technology and digital teams together under one leader,” said Ben Minicucci, CEO of Alaska Air Group, in announcing the news.

— Vijaye Raji , founder and former CEO of Bellevue, Wash.-based Statsig and now OpenAI ’s CTO of applications, has joined the board of Amplitude, a digital analytics and product intelligence company. OpenAI acquired Statsig last year, and Statsig and Amplitude announced a strategic partnership in May in which Amplitude would build on Statsig’s brand and customers.

“Statsig continues as a platform and brand within Amplitude,” Raji said. “Joining the board is an opportunity for me to help carry that mission forward as Amplitude and Statsig build their next chapter together.”

— Vasu Jakkal has left her role as Microsoft corporate vice president of security, compliance, identity, management and privacy after more than six years. She has joined Armadin , a Palo Alto, Calif.-based cybersecurity company, as chief strategy and business officer.

Jakkal is based in the San Francisco Bay Area and previously held executive roles at FireEye and Intel. She praised Armadin’s mission, which she described as building “autonomous security to stay ahead of attackers and build a safer world for all.”

— Microsoft VP Hans Yang is leaving. The Los Angeles-based leader, most recently focused on AI transformation, product strategy and growth, was formerly a general manager for Microsoft for Startups and Microsoft Learn.

“I think my next hill to climb is helping companies capture real ROI from AI,” Yang said , adding, “If you know a company that is struggling to get started with AI, or has invested but is not yet seeing meaningful value, I would welcome any introductions.”

— Venky Chandrasekharan is returning to Microsoft for the role of general manager of Windows commercial category and investments. He left the company in 2021 after 12 years and worked at Qualcomm and Acuity Brands in the interim.

“Having spent some of my most formative years at Microsoft, there’s definitely a sense of familiarity — but I’m coming back with new experiences, a broader perspective, and a lot of excitement for what’s ahead,” Chandrasekharan said .

— Meg O’Conor Bannecker has left Microsoft after two years leading communications for the company’s Washington state team. Past roles include communications leadership at NanoString Technologies, Bannecker Public Affairs and Pier 70 Ventures.

— Patrick Miller has been appointed as global division president of real estate company JLL ’s technology sector. Miller joins from Snap, where he served as senior director of global workplace services. He previously oversaw real estate operations for Amazon’s Seattle-area headquarters for more than three years and has worked for Facebook and DTZ.
“I’ve spent my career on the client side … so I know exactly what it feels like to need a partner who shows up, tells you the truth, and solves real problems,” Miller said .

— DigniFi , a Bellevue, Wash.-based fintech company providing repair financing for autos, RVs, ATVs and other motorized vehicles, has named Jefim Piekarz as chief product officer. Piekarz joins from Arch, and his past employers include Skylab74, Welo, Octane and Etsy. Launched in 2012, DigniFi has facilitated more than $575 million in transactions for automotive merchants in the U.S.
— Seattle-based global logistics company Tideworks Technology has named two C-suite leaders:

— Adaptiva , a Kirkland, Wash.-based company automating software updates across computers, has named Allison Armstrong VP of product marketing. She joined from Elemica and has worked for Transmit Security, Hopin, Qualtrics, Apptio and others.

— Smarsh , a Portland, Ore.-based company providing communications data and insights, has appointed Alessandro Silva as its first chief growth officer. He joins from ACI Worldwide, and his past employers include Western Union and Carlyle Group. Silva is also a board member for Teach for America.

— Seattle-based Yoodli has named Mike Mather as chief learning advisor. The startup recently expanded from helping people practice speeches, sales pitches and job interviews to providing corporate training across wide-ranging skills. Mather is CLO for the accounting firm KPMG US and was previously a partner at EY, IBM and PwC.
“For most of my career, the hardest part of [learning and development] was the gap between training and the moment someone actually has to perform,” Mather said. “Yoodli closes that gap.”

— DigiStor , a company with offices in Austin, Texas, and Vancouver, Wash., that offers secure data storage products, has appointed Peter Bell to its board of directors. Bell co-founded StorageNetworks and serves as managing partner at Stowe Capital, among other roles.

— Seattle-area tech leader Jake Varghese has been promoted to chief product and technology officer for Dayforce , a Minneapolis company providing HR, payroll and related technology. He previously worked for companies including Microsoft, ServiceNow, Tanium and ConnectWise.

— The Association of Washington Business Institute has appointed Meagan Darrow as executive director. Darrow is also an adjunct professor at Evergreen State College and was most recently executive director of the American Diabetes Association. The AWB Institute is the nonprofit research and education affiliate of the association, a longtime organization advocating on behalf of its 8,000 members.

articles.title: Microsoft taps Stripe co-founder John Collison for its board as two longtime directors depart
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: When Stripe co-founder John Collison interviewed Satya Nadella on his company’s podcast last fall, he asked the Microsoft CEO for advice on building a platform business. Collison will soon get to see how Microsoft does it up close.
Collison, 36, the co-founder and president of the Bay Area-based payments platform, has been nominated to Microsoft’s board, the tech giant disclosed Wednesday in its annual proxy statement .

He would fill one of two board seats opening up at Microsoft’s Dec. 8 annual meeting. LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman said in June that he would leave , and the proxy reveals that Disney CFO Hugh Johnston, who chairs the board’s audit committee, is not seeking re-election either. Both have served on the board since 2017 .
The proxy also notes that former EY CEO Carmine Di Sibio, appointed to the board in May , will stand for election by shareholders for the first time.
Microsoft’s board currently has 13 members, including Di Sibio. With Hoffman and Johnston leaving and Collison joining, it will go back to 12, the same number it had before Di Sibio joined in May.

Microsoft says Collison “brings extensive entrepreneurial and operational experience, along with deep expertise in technology.” He started Stripe with his brother, Patrick, in 2010, and businesses using Stripe processed $1.9 trillion in payments in 2025. Collison does not sit on any other public company board.

The board determined that he is independent, after considering ordinary business dealings between Microsoft and companies tied to its directors. The proxy doesn’t mention any business between Microsoft and Stripe, but the two companies already work together.

Stripe helps power Copilot Checkout , which Microsoft launched in January to let U.S. users of its AI assistant buy from Etsy sellers and other retailers without leaving the chat. In 2023, the companies teamed up to let businesses take card payments for paid events in Microsoft Teams.

The companies’ work together came up in the November episode of Stripe’s “Cheeky Pint” podcast. Collison said Stripe was building a platform business in agentic commerce, in which AI agents shop and pay on behalf of people, and asked Nadella what advice he had for a company building in such an early market.
Nadella said the key would be making it simple for small merchants to sell through AI agents, without asking them to set up servers or adopt a string of new technical protocols themselves.
The relationship goes back years. Nadella said he first visited Stripe’s San Francisco office when he was running Microsoft’s cloud business, before he became CEO.

He said Stripe reminded Microsoft of something it had once been good at, “following the developer, being where the startups are,” and said that thinking “led me even to GitHub,” the code-sharing platform Microsoft acquired in 2018 for $7.5 billion .

articles.title: Endurance Energy hits a brief milestone in its quest for undersea geothermal power
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Endurance Energy says its prototype marine geothermal power system generated more electricity than it consumed during a recent deployment 300 miles off the Oregon coast — though the milestone lasted just 8.7 seconds.

The Seattle-based startup landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent releasing water at about 538 degrees Fahrenheit. The team operated the system remotely through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed.
The expedition marked Endurance’s fifth deployment to the ocean floor where it tested Adélie — a 100-kilowatt geothermal generator named for a penguin.

The company is part of a broader race to harness geothermal energy, using heat from water or steam under the Earth’s crust, converted into electricity. But while companies such as Fervo and Sage Geosystems focus on terrestrial sites, Endurance is the first commercial venture pursuing undersea sources.
“The main question we had is can the system generate more power than it uses,” Andrew Redd , Endurance’s founder and CEO, said in a statement about the expedition, which began last month.
“Adélie did,” he added. “Goddard’s first liquid-fueled rocket flew for two and a half seconds. Our first net-positive run lasted about nine. Our approach is to make it exist, then make it good.”
The test produced only a brief burst of surplus electricity, reaching a peak net output of 16.5 kilowatts. Challenges with the technology and a failure of a power cable cut the dive short.

The team also drilled what it called the world’s first geothermal well. At a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface, its machinery created two bore holes that tapped into hydrothermal fluid. It capped one hole and drilled a roughly 2-inch wide, 52-foot deep geothermal well at the other. While the well delivered hot fluid, it wasn’t suited for testing the energy system, sending the team to the natural vent.

Endurance said the expedition included voluntary environmental monitoring. The team mapped the seafloor to select the least disruptive test site, sampled water before and after operations, surveyed marine life and monitored sound.

While the startup has made rapid progress, its approach faces significant challenges: high pressure and corrosive conditions, mineral buildup inside equipment and the risk of costly repairs to seafloor machinery. And although many population centers sit near coastlines, the systems would still need expensive subsea cables to carry electricity over potentially long distances.
The company has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three-dozen employees.
This winter, Endurance plans to deploy Gentoo, a refurbished and upgraded version of Adélie designed to generate more power for longer periods.
The company is also developing its first commercial project in Tonga, with the goal of delivering its first electricity in 2027.

articles.title: Rinck Pushes Against Gender-Based Violence, Facing Budget Headwinds
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: In the middle of a Seattle budget season marked by councilmember complaints and hyperbole, Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck has stepped forward to announce her “Seattle Stands With Survivors, Every Step” campaign. While anti-survivor rhetoric continues to pervade the national news, the federal government under President Donald Trump is cutting key investments that have historically supported survivors of gender-based violence – and Rinck wants Seattle to step in to help fill the gaps.

“Every two minutes, someone in this country is sexually assaulted,” Rinck said to kick off her press conference on Wednesday. “We cannot be serious about public safety in this city without also being serious about gender-based violence.”

“I stand here as your Seattle City Council member representing the Office of Position 8 and as a survivor myself,” Rinck continued. “I know what it costs to say those words out loud, but I know what it means when someone believes you and when someone is there to walk alongside of you. Every survivor in Seattle deserves that.”

Rinck wants to make $8 million in investments for survivors of gender-based violence in the 2027-2028 biennial budget to stabilize and scale up programs in three key areas: accountability for abusers and justice for survivors, direct survivor services, and prevention.

Rinck will also introduce a Statement of Legislative Intent (SLI) in order to help guide the work around funding and supporting these services in her Human Services, Labor, & Economic Development committee next year.

At her press conference, Rinck was flanked by fellow Councilmembers Dionne Foster, Eddie Lin, and Bob Kettle, as well as Seattle City Attorney Erika Evans, King County Councilmember Jorge Barón, State Representative Darya Farivar, and current LD-37 candidate for the State House Jaelynn Scott. Also present were many of the service providers with whom Rinck has been consulting to better understand the current needs in order to develop her campaign.

Riddhi Mukopadhyay, the executive director at the Sexual Violence Law Center (SVLC), said the average number of legal problems a Seattle resident who has survived domestic violence or sexual assault will experience is 19.7.

“Survivors cannot rely on the criminal system alone. Justice denied shows up costing more and hurting more,” Mukopadhyay said. “That's why community programs and legal services like ours matter. It's the collaborative network here that quietly keeps people housed, safe, employed, and in school. We don't make the headlines, but we do make the difference.”

Rinck spoke of the Jeffrey Epstein survivors who have spent years fighting to be heard, the case of the Cornell Seven gang rape , and the comedian opening Saturday Night Live by calling women who wear shorts in the gym “whores.”
“Three stories, one clear message to survivors,” Rinck said. “We don't believe you. It doesn't matter. Our fear and pain is just a joke.”

Rinck also mentioned the woman who was raped by a fraternity member at the University of Washington in 2022, who recently filed a suit against the university for failing to protect her from a known offender.

“ I think that as we see the national news over the last several years, and we see the lack of accountability, the amount of corruption, and lack of consequence for this very significant and profound harm that survivors are experiencing, I think it's incredibly meaningful to have elected leaders and and local communities responding very unequivocally that this is not okay, and we need to actually make sure that survivors have resources and have support,” Amarinthia Torres, the co-executive director of the Coalition Ending Gender-Based Violence, told The Urbanist .
Feminist Soraya Chemaly linked the problem of pervasive campus rape directly to our society’s widespread patterns of impunity and lack of accountability.

“What I’m describing is [a] closed loop of institutional self-preservation, power, and elite freedom from accountability,” Chemaly wrote . “The mechanisms evident in cases of sexual violence — diffusing moral culpability and liability, protecting influential and powerful classes of people, forcing victims to absorb costs as individuals — are the same as those we see across corporate and political institutions that pervasively externalize the costs and violence required to maintain unaccountable power and a life with no limits for a few.”

In a period some people consider to be a backlash to the #MeToo movement, the news contains a litany of stories involving the Trump administration: the scandal of the Epstein files showing a web of power with a convicted child sex offender at its heart, the White House intervening on behalf of accused sex trafficker Andrew Tate, Russell Brand moderating a recent panel at a recent Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) summit right before going on trial for multiple allegations of rape and sexual assault, and Trump’s own civil liability for sexual abuse (a legal finding before he was elected to the presidency for the second time) as well as the scores of allegations of sexual misconduct.
Meanwhile, headlines decry the influence of the “manosphere” and its impact on violence rates against women and children.

Within this context, Trump’s administration has moved decisively in cutting financial support for survivors of gender-based violence, which is having impacts across the country and in Seattle specifically.

In addition to cutting social safety net programs like Medicaid and SNAP, which assist survivors in trying to rebuild their lives, H.R. 1 cut over $200 million from the Office on Violence Against Women as well as survivor-specific assistance within the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). In the last two years, there have also been cuts to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention funding for violence prevention research, Department of Justice (DoJ) cuts to funding and training for child sex trafficking investigations and an attempt to cease grant-giving to organizations involved in Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) work, and cuts to the Prison Rape Elimination Act.

In the wake of the Cornell gang rape investigation being re-opened, the Trump administration weakened the Title IX rules reverting to stricter guidelines for formal complaints and procedures and r emoving protections for LGBTQ+ students . Former President Joe Biden had strengthened these rules in 2024.

“It's important to note that many folks who disproportionately experience gender-based violence are marginalized and often erased people, and folks who are already under attack by other national policies right now,” Rinck told The Urbanist . “I'm thinking about immigrant women, women of color broadly, trans people, just to name a few.”

Rinck wanted to bring attention to the local impacts of the federal cuts, which include Aurora Commons reducing the service hours of its Safe, Healthy, Empowered (S.H.E.) Clinic, Salvation Army and New Beginnings anticipating major cuts to domestic violence transitional housing, and ReWA dealing with federal funding cuts to legal assistance and housing services for refugee and immigrant survivors. Some organizations are opting out of all DOJ grants due to the concern about possible restrictions around DEI values.

“We really see the root causes of gender-based violence being about rigid gender and gender inequity, so abuses of power and disparity,” Torres said. “And I think that those root causes are really important to name as we think about how we address harm when harm happens and when violence happens because the folks that are the most vulnerable, that are the most marginalized, that are the most objectified, that is when violence is occurring, is to those folks that are most on the margins and where we see dehumanization and objectification occurring.”

Organizations serving transgender people are seeing lessened philanthropic support, meaning fewer resources for transgender people who have survived gender-based violence. The ability for organizations to serve unaccompanied immigrant children who are often victims of gender-based violence has dramatically diminished. Immigrants who are survivors are afraid that if they share about their abuse or try to get help, they might be deported, Torres said.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson’s 2027 budget proposal ends some one-time investments in this space, including $500,000 for gender-based violence services and $400,000 for commercial sexual exploitation work, as well as a $285,000 cut to the Office of Civil Rights program providing funding for community-led domestic violence response and prevention programs. These are some of the investments Rinck is looking to restore.
Rinck told The Urbanist she’s also looking to restore federal cuts to help stabilize programs and to help programs improve their staffing ratios.

Separate from Rinck’s $8 million plan, Foster will be introducing an amendment for a one-time budget add of $1 million to help address the Seattle City Attorney’s Office’s backlog of domestic violence and other cases. Seattle City Attorney Erika Evans shared that of the 5,000 case backlog inherited from her predecessor Ann Davison, 1,700 of them are domestic violence cases, referencing a recent case that had taken almost two years to be filed.

Seattle’s October revenue forecast , delivered last Friday, was not as rosy as some councilmembers might have hoped. From 2026-2028, the forecast predicted only $8.8 million in total additional revenues, meaning the city council will have very little wiggle room to fund their priorities in the current budget proposal without also implementing cuts.

“I would consider this a bad forecast, even though it could be much worse. This is one of the smallest increases in the last several years,” Budget Chair Dan Strauss told The Urbanist . “We are being asked to do more with less. The federal government continues to try and defund basic services, from SNAP benefits to permanent supportive housing. While we received a very small revenue increase in this forecast, Seattle is also being forced to take on more financial responsibility for doing the federal government’s job.”

Councilmember Bob Kettle has been vocal in criticizing Wilson’s budget proposal, particularly as it pertains to public safety: primarily the Seattle Police Department (SPD) and the Seattle Fire Department (SFD). Kettle has expressed particular concern over the plateau – at 1,250 officers – in SPD staffing that would occur at the end of next year, given that he believes the City requires 1,400 officers or more.
Some councilmembers also expressed concern that more money wasn’t being invested in the Unified Care Team that performs sweeps of unhoused people around the City.

Given the budget crunch, it is unclear if Kettle would have the votes to further fund a police department that is already receiving a larger increase in investment than any other City department under Wilson’s proposal. There does seem to be a stronger consensus amongst councilmembers to try to reverse the $7.1 million cut to SFD’s overtime budget.

A spokesperson from SFD clarified to The Urbanist that the unit outages it experienced in 2025 were unplanned, as opposed to the planned outages that would be taking place under the overtime restriction in 2027.

“As a result of unplanned unit outages in 2025, the department reinvested some of that funding in areas that surpassed their planned budget, including workers compensation (as a result of personnel injuries), minor equipment costs (as a result of inflation), and fleet maintenance and repair,” the SFD spokesperson said.
Last week, Central Staff member Ann Gorman told the council the unplanned 2025 SFD unit outages didn’t appear to impact response times.

The almost-flat budget forecast might not bode well for Rinck to be able to garner enough support from her colleagues to add $8 million in funding over the next two years for gender-based violence programs. Rinck assured The Urbanist she intends to fight for the investment, but she sees the campaign as a multi-year effort that will also involve work within her committee.

“We're daylighting this issue because we need to talk about gender-based violence,” Rinck said. “Far too many of the messages that women in the U.S. have gotten in the past week – past two weeks, past year, if I'm being honest – have been that gender-based violence and forms of sexual violence attached to that: people who perpetuate that will not be held accountable, or that people don't care, or that this is just a joke. And I think it's tremendously important that people in positions of power right now send a different message that we're actually not going to tolerate that, and we are going to hold you accountable.”
“Everybody knows a survivor of gender-based violence,” Torres said.

articles.title: That ‘just one more try’ feeling: Capitol Hill ‘clawcade’ Chibi Tings now open
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Those cheers you are hearing on E Pine might be coming from Chibi Tings , a new Japanese-style “clawcade.”

The new, all-ages Capitol Hill arcade features claw machines, giant gashapon dispensers, and blind boxes in a mix of collecting, tactile problem-solving, and social entertainment that only kurēn gēmu can provide.
“It’s not just for kids. It’s for grown-ups who still love arcade lights, capsule surprises, and that ‘just one more try’ feeling,” the arcade’s promo reads.

The arcade’s debut has double-upped the all-ages good times on the block. Chibi Tings neighbors The Tilted Table — the arcade bar and tabletop gaming hangout that has grown out of new ownership of the longtime Raygun Lounge. The space has previously been home to the Kpop Nara boutique before the shop made a classic Capitol Hill move to E Pike.
Chibi Tings is owned by Brent Hanada , a first-time Capitol Hill entrepreneur.

Chibi Tings and Tilted are part of a robust assortment of Capitol Hill pinball and arcade venues including Capitol Hill carnival bar Unicorn and its Narwhal underground sibling, and 10th Ave’s 21+ dedicated arcade bar , Time Warp .

The overhaul of a Broadway axe-tossing venue will add another as the space becomes home to the Seattle location of the growing Recess adult play and multi-attraction social hub concept . This update from Kansas City’s Arcade Supernova shows some of the goodies being installed on Broadway. The company restores, maintains, and rotates vintage 1980s/1990s arcade cabinets and pinball machines and is now adding the Seattle Recess location to its roster.

Back on E Pine, Chibi (ちび or チビ) is a Japanese slang term meaning “small,” “short,” or “tiny.” In pop culture, anime, and manga, it describes an art style often called “super-deformed” where characters are rendered in an exaggerated, cute, miniature form with oversized heads, large expressive eyes, and tiny bodies.

Crane games are ubiquitous across Japan but they operate at scale, anchoring multi-story arcade centers run by major brands like GiGO , Taito , and Round1 . Unlike Western machines that rely on payout algorithms and generic plush, Japanese UFO Catchers function as skill games offering prize-only anime figures and licensed collectibles that can’t be bought at standard retail. The venues are famous for floor attendants who help reposition stubborn prizes for struggling players. The machines also typically accept coins or transit IC cards.

While you can’t tap your ORCA card at Chibi Tings, the arcade’s bright lights and buzzing machines whir with the same fun and workers are part of the hullaballoo. “We cheer wins,” Chibi Tings promises.

The E Pine venue operates on a token system called “tings” where a $20 buy-in typically provides enough plays to win a few prizes across their lineup of traditional Japanese UFO catchers, mini claws, giant instant-win gashapon capsule dispensers, and curated blind-box stations stocked with imported plushies, anime collectibles, and specialty Asian snacks.
Chibi Tings is open at 501 E Pine. Learn more at chibitings.com .

articles.title: League of Women Voters holding Central District ‘Ballot Party’
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: The League of Women Voters of Seattle-King County will host a family-friendly “Ballot Party” on Sunday, October 25th from 11 AM to 2 PM at the Garfield Community Center .

Co-hosted with the Urban League of Metropolitan Seattle, Delta Sigma Theta Seattle Chapter, and the Central Area Neighborhood District Council , the drop-in event invites residents to review sample ballots, make voting plans, and complete their ballots alongside neighbors ahead of the November 3 General Election.
The gathering will also offer coffee, snacks, and children’s activities.
“Plenty of people who skip a midterm aren’t apathetic. They’re unsure,” said League Development Chair Susan Waller . “We can fix unsure.”
What: Ballot Party , a drop-in event to make a voting plan, get answers and fill in ballots
When: Sunday, Oct. 25, 11 am to 2 pm. Drop in anytime.
Where: Garfield Community Center, 2323 East Cherry St., Seattle
On the table: Snacks, beverages and coffee, sample ballots, children’s activities and conversation about what’s on the ballot
CHS reported here on the major issues Capitol Hill and Central District voters will decide on in November. You can find all CHS Election coverage at capitolhillseattle.com/tag/elections/
The General Election is Tuesday, November 3rd.

articles.title: Land use review underway for Broadway Crisis Center overhaul
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A key land use process has begun as officials aim for a planned end of 2027 opening of the Central Crisis Care Center emergency mental health facility on Broadway.

The Master Use Permit application for the 1110 Harvard Ave medical facility marks an important regulatory milestone in King County’s $56 million push to transform the three-story former Polyclinic building.
“The Project consist of the renovate an existing building into an acute behavior health care center,” the paperwork begins.

A Master Use Permit serves as the city’s official land-use gatekeeper, legally establishing changes in building use and occupancy before physical construction permits can be issued. According to project filings submitted on behalf of property owner King County, the renovation will convert the site into an acute behavioral health facility designed to maintain a “no wrong door’ approach” and an “open-door, 24/7 walk-in policy to serve all individuals who come to the center.”
Project plans call for interior and exterior upgrades that “apply the principles of trauma-informed design, and recognize the unique needs of individuals across the lifespan.”

The MUP also formalizes substantial exterior and access reconfigurations. it proposes eliminating 17 existing on-site parking stalls to rely on two proposed accessible on-street spaces, while managing more than 2,000 square feet of earth disturbance across public rights-of-way on Harvard, Broadway, and E Union as entrances to the facility are reconfigured.
The south end has been an empty lot for decades (Image: City of Seattle)
The plan does not specify any planned upgrades or use of the parcel’s empty southern portion long ago home to the Scottish Rite Cathedral .

Litigation and administrative appeals can delay or halt a Seattle Master Use Permit though the legal threshold required to substantially alter or kill a project is high. In most cases, litigation forces additional environmental studies, or extracts design concessions rather than outright stopping a permitted land use.
For renovation projects like 1110 Harvard Ave, standard building work without major exterior expansions or rezoning applications have limited targets for appeal.
On top of the $41.5 million acquisition cost of the building, officials have earmarked $11.5 million to $14.5 million in spending for renovation and operational start-up costs.
Recent filings also will enroll the property in the city’s Vacant Building Monitoring program as medical use of the building winds down.
This land use review intersects with neighborhood public safety efforts.

As the citizen-led Seattle Community Advisory Group formed to help shape planning for the project works to allocate a $3 million county mitigation fund to address street disorder and crime gaps, MUP filings dictate physical crime prevention through environmental design updates including sidewalk grading, frontage lighting, and secure access corridors.

CHS reported on the advisory group’s early work around public safety improvements focused heavily on surrounding street conditions. During an April session, members raised worries over “open-air drug markets, gun violence, property crime, and disorder,” warning that without strong post-crisis discharge planning, “people across King County could concentrate issues in Capitol and First Hill.”

CHS reported here on the 2025 approval of the $56 million plan to acquire the property, overhaul the building, and hire an operator for what is planned to be the second in a network of five county facilities providing 24-7 walk-in and emergency care mental health clinics funded by a 2023 voter-approved levy.
Last November , CHS reported on the selection of Connections Health Solutions to operate the center.
With officials targeting an opening in late 2027 now at the earliest, securing MUP approval is a critical step needed to clear contractor bidding and keep renovations on schedule.
