articles.title: An Incomplete History of the Millionaires Tax
articles.author: John Stang
paras: Perhaps the biggest issue on the ballot this fall is the fate of the Millionaires Tax. To change Washington’s regressive tax system or to not change it? That is the question.

Initiative 645, an initiative effort from Let’s Go Washington, the group behind the other anti-trans and anti-LGBTQ initiatives on the ballot, would repeal the Millionaires Tax, which is expected to raise $3 billion annually by taxing roughly 21,000 eligible Washington households. Repealing it would lose millions of dollars for funding for schools, health care, and other critical services.

The whole purpose of the Millionaires Tax was to find more state funding in a time when unaffordability has reached an all-time high. It could also pave the way for more progressive tax reform. But first the tax must withstand the multiple challenges against it, including this initiative effort, which has raised millions to oppose it. A campaign to counter I-645 has far outfundraised the repeal effort.

The pro-tax side believes repealing it would be devastating. Adam Glickman, secretary-treasurer of SEIU 775, which represents service workers, says the initiative “would cut critical services that people rely on.”

According to Washington Education Association president Janie White, “The Millionaires Tax would help the state fund schools, health care, services for seniors and people with disabilities, and more.” Some of that funding could pay for special education, additional staffing, and behavioral health resources.
Pivotally, keeping the Millionaires Tax would enable the state to trim its high sales tax, which disproportionately affects the lower income brackets, according to Glickman.

You’ve heard it over and over: Washington has the second most regressive tax system in the country. The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) mapped out this regressiveness in a 2024 report .

In Washington in 2024, ITEP said the top 1 percent earned more than $878,400 in a year and paid an estimated 4.1 percent of its income in state taxes. The next 19 percent earned $162,000 to $878,400 annually, paying 9.3 percent or less of its income in state taxes. That also meant that less than 20 percent of Washington’s taxpayers earned more than $250,000—a new key political benchmark—that year. The bottom 20 percent earned less than $33,500 a year, while paying 13.8 percent of its income in state taxes.
For many years, legislators talked about fixing this regressiveness, but never did. Until last year.

The Millionaires Tax was born from the 2025 legislative session when Democratic legislative leaders determined that the state government would need more money. Then President Donald Trump passed his “One Big Beautiful Bill.”
“Enormous tax cuts for corporations and the really wealthy individuals added fuel to the fire,” says state Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen, D-Washington.

Trump’s bill cut taxes for the rich, plus health and social programs. It was so dire, it supposedly put moderate legislators and their constituents in the mood to tax the incomes of Washington’s wealthiest residents for the first time in decades, Democratic leaders speculated.
So, Pedersen and other Democratic leaders seized the moment. They had to convince both leftists and moderates to pass the complicated Millionaires Tax bill. Every Republican was dead set against it.
Pedersen remembered being nervous. “I wasn’t confident it would get through the House till a few days before it passed,” he says.

They had to convince moderates that any income tax wasn’t a kiss of death. The struggling economy and Trump’s bill helped persuade them. Leftists wanted and got major changes in the bill. They stripped out a $550 million tax break for large companies. They moved a sunset of an expansion of the sales tax on services from 2030 to 2029. The legislature eliminated a sales tax on diapers and boosted a working family tax credit. The final version of the tax puts a 9.9 percent tax on persons earning more than $1 million a year, with the first $1 million being exempt. The state plans to start collecting the tax in 2029 on 2028 incomes.

Aside from the realities of the economic hellscape, the timing for the Millionaires Tax was also right because of the current Washington State Supreme Court. The legislative Democrats thought the court might be ready to reverse or modify a 1933 ruling that has stood in the way of a state income tax for nearly a century. The tax could be the bomb to blow up that ruling.

The key words are “income tax” and “graduated.” Written in 1889, Washington’s constitution does not contain the phrase “income tax”—a fringe idea in the 19th century. The 1889 constitution does address “property taxes,” including the fact that the same property tax rate must apply equally to everyone.

Washington adopted its first income tax in 1932. The next year, the state supreme court ruled an income tax is also a property tax, and since that income tax was levied at different rates for different incomes, the 1933 court ruled it unconstitutional.

Over time, the word “graduated” faded from the state’s political memory. Meanwhile, the words “income tax” became kryptonite to the state’s legislators and voters. Make no mistake, the 2026 millionaires’ income tax is a graduated tax. Pedersen hopes today’s supreme court is more comfortable with the idea that property and income taxes are separate entities than their 1933 counterparts. The court’s ruling could change the state’s tax code.

But in early April, former state attorney general Rob McKenna, former Supreme Court justice Phil Talmadge, and the Citizen Action Defense Fund filed a lawsuit in Klickitat County arguing that earlier rulings by the Washington State Supreme Court have set a strong precedent that an income tax is a property tax.
Pedersen acknowledged: “It’s a big thing to strike down a precedent.”
McKenna and Jackson Maynard, head of the Citizen Action Defense Fund, each donated $500 to the anti-tax ballot initiative.

Conservative interests are financially supporting state supreme court candidates they believe will kill the tax when it inevitably hits the high court. Meanwhile, liberal interests are doing the same thing with a different slate of candidates.
If that conservative strategy to kill the tax doesn’t work, there’s always the ballot measure.

Yes on I-645, the group trying to repeal the tax, has raised almost $6 million. They’ve spent nearly $4 million of that so far, much of it on just getting enough signatures to get the repeal measure on November’s ballot.
Spread across two political action committees, the big money against the Millionaires Tax comes from the usual suspects: a handful of wealthy people and business interests on the anti-tax side.

The biggest donors to the PAC are hedge fund manager Brian Heywood ($545,000) and retired trucking company executive Steve Gordon ($275,000), the leaders of Let’s Go Washington, the group behind this initiative and the other two initiatives on the ballot. The rest of the list includes Steve’s parents, Larry and Virgina Gordon ($450,000), retired tech multimillionaire Lawrence Hughes ($250,000), the investment firm Madrona Venture Group ($250,000), and Bellevue shopping center developer and landlord Kemper Holdings ($200,000).

Those seven contributed $1.97 million of the almost $6 million the PAC has collected. Several people and business interests donated in five figures, plus numerous smaller individual donors. Microsoft Azure president Girish Bablani donated $1,000.
The side supporting the tax, No on I-645 and another PAC, have massively out-fundraised the Yes campaign. They’ve raised roughly $12.8 million.

Unions are the main bankrollers of the pro-tax side—spread across three PACs. These include various branches of the Washington Education Association ($3.14 million), SEIU 775 ($1.64 million), the National Education Association ($1 million), and the Washington Federation of State Employees ($1 million). Contributions under a million came from the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees ($500,000), UFCW 3000 ($250,000), and the Washington State Nurses Association ($100,000). The only individual in the top donors is retired software developer and current official of a philanthropic organization David Habib, who donated $150,000. Habib and the six unions account for $7.8 million of the total $12.8 million raised by the Millionaires Tax supporters.
That should be enough to counter the repeal campaign. But its talking points are persuasive.
Along with the $6 million that Yes on I-645’s two PACs have raised, the anti-tax movement is also relying on a few key talking points to win voters to its side.
One major argument against the tax is that the Millionaires Tax is a gateway drug to an income tax on the everyman, not just millionaires.

“Senator Pedersen has made his desire for a universal statewide income tax abundantly clear. In no uncertain terms, he has outlined that he will do whatever it takes to change the law to pass an income tax for all residents. What he fails to understand is that voters don’t trust Olympia with their money,” said Hallie Herzberg, spokeswoman for Let’s Go Washington.

Tax opponents point to a recent KUOW interview with State Rep. Cindy Ryu, D-Shoreline, who is running for the state senate. She argued the income threshold should be lowered from $1 million to $250,000.

Pedersen pushed back against this narrative. According to him, the Democrats don’t have the long-term political capital to lower the tax’s threshold from $1 million. He pointed to Gov. Bob Ferguson saying last legislative session that he would veto any bill that lowered the $1 million tax threshold. Pedersen also believed that those necessary Democratic moderate votes wouldn’t support lowering the threshold for many years because of the potential political blowback.

The other high-profile argument against the Millionaires Tax is that it will drive business leaders and high earners out of state. While this phenomenon has been studied nationally, local research is scarce. Almost all evidence of an elite exodus from Washington is anecdotal.

“Every day we receive messages from people who have left, or are preparing to leave. We have real estate agents telling us that people are putting their homes on the market. There are news stories weekly about the wealthy leaving and taking their businesses with them,” says Morgan Irwin, the Association of Washington Business’s vice president of government affairs.

The AWB routinely surveys its members. The latest took place this July, with 378 responses out of roughly 8,000 members. That’s 4 percent of their membership. The respondents were the only people who wanted to volunteer an opinion, as opposed to having a truly random poll.

Thirty-three percent of those respondents say they plan to expand their businesses outside of Washington, chiefly because of this state’s overall tax situation—the new Millionaires Tax plus several other new taxes. Forty-five percent of the business owners plan to move out of Washington themselves.

articles.title: Seattle City Council Passes Draconian Effective RV Ban
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: Last night, the Seattle City Council passed the most comprehensive reform of large vehicle regulations in a generation to make it harder for homeless people to live in RVs and trailers. The six ordinances sponsored by Councilmember Dan Strauss will require people living in large vehicles to obtain a permit to park for more than two hours. Even with a permit, they’ll still have to move every 72 hours.

The legislative package aims to assuage longstanding complaints about sanitation and livability issues caused by RV residents in industrial neighborhoods while increasing outreach and services to the historically overlooked segment of Seattle’s homeless population.

However, many RV residents and homelessness advocates say the permitting system is a ban in disguise, and will just further hurt people already living on the margins, forcing them to either leave the city or get rid of what little property they still own.

The two most controversial bills in the legislative package, including the new permitting system, passed 6 to 3 at last night’s meeting, cleanly following the council’s ideological faultline. Mayor Katie Wilson hasn’t taken an official stance on the legislation, but expressed concerns about the costs of rolling out the new permitting system. If she chose to veto the bills, the council would have the votes to override it.

The Seattle bills mirror legislation recently passed by other municipalities like San Francisco, part of a nationwide crackdown on unsheltered homelessness in the wake of the 2024 Grants Pass decision.

While Strauss’s legislation is framed as a permitting system, it amounts to nothing less than a wholesale ban on RV living in Seattle, says Graham Pruss, executive director of the National Vehicle Residency Coalition.

The permitting system will only be available to people included in a one-time survey of vehicle residents. To obtain the permit, they’ll also have to maintain a valid vehicle registration—a significant hurdle for many—and ensure their RV or trailer is of habitable condition. Many homeless Seattleites live in dilapidated or rusty vehicles legally considered “junk” and ineligible for a permit.
Moreover, the permit won’t create a permanent legal status for RV dwellers; it can be revoked after six refusals of “appropriate” offers of shelter.
Strauss told The Stranger the phase out mechanism of the permitting system is by design—he doesn’t want Seattle to be seen as a destination for vehicle residents.
“If we were to leave the census open perpetually or forever, my fear is that we would have RVs coming from all of the Pacific Northwest, from Idaho to Oregon,” Strauss says.

In a letter to the council, the Seattle/King County Coalition on Homelessness criticized the new permitting program and called on it to reject four out of the six bills. It said the funding for eight new staffers to enforce the permits was a bad use of taxpayer money and should instead go to direct outreach.

The coalition did support several aspects of Strauss’s proposal, including additional funding for outreach and the establishment of dedicated city-managed parking for RVs and trailers so that homeless residents entering shelter won’t have to get rid of their vehicles.

While a majority of homelessness service providers and advocates opposed the permitting system, the UHeights Vehicle Residency Outreach (VRO) came out in support of the legislation. VRO did not respond to a request for comment. Other supporters of the legislation, including a member of the Ballard Alliance and a representative of the North Lake neighbors group, testified in support of the legislation.

Pruss said that Strauss used promises of funding have been used as a “tool” to divide service providers and make the effective RV ban politically palatable. “For that funding, the rest of the folks who live in RVs in perpetuity are being banished from Seattle and the larger region of the Puget Sound,” he says.

Pruss warned that Seattle’s legislation will set off a wave of bans as RV residents get displaced outside city limits. That phenomenon has been playing out in the Bay Area, where a third of RV residents have already moved outside San Francisco since it passed its ban last summer.

Adding to the concerns is the lack of an active safe lot for vehicle residents within Seattle. The Low Income Housing Institute’s (LIHI) Salmon Bay safe lot was forced to close in May 2025 (it was turned into a pickleball facility). Safe lots make living in RVs easier, allowing residents to connect to power and sewage and be part of a stable community without the fear of being swept. LIHI plans to open its new Glassyard Commons site, serving 72 vehicles and 20 tiny houses, next month.
In her budget proposal, Wilson allocated funding for a second safe lot. Strauss says he is sponsoring a budget amendment to ensure that funding is included.

Even if both safe lots are operational, they won’t be able to serve all of Seattle’s RV residents. In this year’s Point-in-Time Count, UW researchers found that on any given night nearly 4,000 people are living in their vehicles across King County, including more than 600 in large vehicles such as RVs.
LIHI boasts that 60 percent of the 87 people who lived in the Salmon Bay safe lot eventually got permanent housing.

But for Tiffany Taylor, who is one of the 40 percent who didn’t end up with a home, Salmon Bay ended with bitter disappointment. While she appreciated the accommodations during her time in the safe lot, including the ability to keep her trailer, she had to get rid of it when Salmon Bay suddenly closed.

Instead of housing, LIHI offered her a place in one of its tiny houses. Taylor estimates that the trailer was worth about $9,000 when she moved into the safe lot. She says she was okay with the tradeoff as long as she ended up getting placed in an apartment.

However, earlier this summer, she got kicked out of her tiny house for having an unauthorized AC system, leaving her completely homeless once again. Taylor says that in order for the new RV permitting system to work, it will need to ensure people like her don’t fall through the cracks

“They need to do a better job of making sure that people are really taken care of and not just cycled out and left with nothing,” Taylor said. “Like now I’m just out there trying to figure it out all from ground zero.”

articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: Welcome back to Pop Loser! This week, unexpected worlds collided: Bono and Dan Savage, John Wilson and Harry Styles, and David Byrne and Oliva Rodrigo. Joni Mitchell can now vote in the US. Plus, a shout-out to the cool goth working at Double Dare Records in Burien who was blasting Switchblade Symphony on Saturday morning.
This week in Strangerland, l ocal hip-hop group 4ust Collective stopped by the office for another episode of Noise Complaint .

Bono quoted Dan Savage. While a part of me hoped that the quote involved pegging, “fucking first,” or dangers of being in a PUD (Poly Under Duress) relationship, Bono revealed it was Savage’s powerful insight regarding the AIDS crisis that helped inspire U2’s new album, Carnaval De Luz . Bono told the New York Times : “There’s a Dan Savage quote about when he was an AIDS activist in San Francisco in the middle of that crisis. He said: ‘In the morning, we would bury our friends. In the afternoon, we’d go out to protest so we’d have less people to bury. Then, in the evenings, we would go out and dance, because the dance was what we were fighting for.’ I loved that so much. That is not surrendering to the melancholy. That’s the defiance.”

Joni Mitchell can now vote in the US. In an Instagram post shared last Tuesday, Mitchell announced that after a 62-year-long journey, she’s officially become a US citizen. On Thursday, she posted another statement to socials, clarifying to the haters that she became a citizen so that she could vote: “I didn’t give up my Canadian citizenship, and I never will,” she wrote. “I’m a proud Canerican like Neil Young.”

The History of Harry . I think this is a fun idea, and with Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter Live at Carnegie Hall dropping next month, it seems like film auteurs making concert movies is back in style. Billy Joel might never perform again. On Thursday, the Piano Man sent a health update to The Hollywood Reporter . “What the neurologist told me, every time you do a show, it’s like you’re getting a concussion,” Joel disclosed, adding that he currently isn’t allowed to drive, and won’t know if he can get back on stage or his beloved motorcycles until further testing is done. Joel underwent surgery early last year and canceled his remaining tour dates following a diagnosis of hydrocephalus, a neurological condition that has impacted his balance.

articles.title: Chiricahua is the nation’s newest national park – what does that mean?
articles.author:
<name>Seth T. Kannarr, Visiting Honors Lecturer, Southern Illinois University Edwardsville</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/seth-t-kannarr-1390874"/>
paras: With a stroke of a pen, President Donald Trump has officially created the United States’ 64th national park .

Chiricahua , in southeastern Arizona, was established as a national monument in April 1924 to protect its towering rhyolite hoodoos – tall spires of rock – and diversity of wildlife. The mountainous landscape is commonly known as a “wonderland of rocks.”

An act of Congress , signed by Trump, has now designated the 12,000-acre property a national park, the flagship label of the National Park Service system. It joins the Grand Canyon , Petrified Forest and Saguaro as the fourth national park in Arizona.

As a geographer who studies parks and the naming of places, I have seen that when a National Park Service property is redesignated as a national park, the new label doesn’t typically include much change for the site itself beyond signs and branding.

There’s not usually more money available to manage or protect the site. But the new title serves political purposes and could mean quite a lot to visitors, supporters and surrounding communities alike in the coming years.

The National Park Service manages 433 properties, which it calls units , with 19 different designations , such as “national battlefields,” “national lakeshores” and “national scenic trails.” Only 64 of these units carry the formal title or designation of “national park.”
All but one of these categories can be bestowed only by Congress. National monuments can be created by the president directly, under the provisions of the Antiquities Act of 1906 .

For example, the Antiquities Act has been at the center of a decade-long controversy over the size of Bears Ears National Monument , which President Barack Obama created to protect 1.3 million acres in Utah in December 2016. That same act allowed Trump to shrink the protected area to 200,000 acres in 2017 and President Joe Biden to reexpand it to 1.3 million acres in 2021. In 2026, Trump slashed it again, to 121,000 acres .

My previous analysis of the contentious redesignation of the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial in St. Louis to Gateway Arch National Park in 2018 found that it was not done to offer additional protection for this monument to the United States’ Western exploration and growth.
Rather, the move was meant to take advantage of the public significance of the “national park” label and thereby attract more tourists and tourism revenue to the local economy.

The effort to make it a national park was part of a local campaign to renovate the underground visitor center , revitalize the park grounds and increase tourism. But the law that formalized the change included no additional funding, resources or protections for the Gateway Arch.

Changing the designation contradicted the park service’s own declaration that the term “national park” should be used for an area that “ contains a variety of resources and encompasses large land or water areas to help provide adequate protection of the resources.”

During congressional hearings, the deputy director of the National Park Service, Robert Vogel, recommended the Gateway Arch not be labeled a national park but rather a national monument, because it “ is too small and limited in the range of resources the site protects and interprets to be called a national park.”

Gateway Arch National Park is now the smallest-area park in the U.S., at less than 200 acres, and is home to a large steel arch, an open lawn area, a museum and a single historic building – a courthouse where one of the Dred Scott trials was heard, along with other civil rights cases.

However, it does not provide opportunities to view wildlife in its natural habitat, spectacular geologic features, diverse outdoor recreation opportunities or a sense of wilderness that the public has come to expect from national parks .
The park’s website admits “ it is unusual for a national park to have no natural plant life ” and describes the park as adjacent to the “ concrete jungle of downtown St. Louis .”

Although Chiricahua’s rocky landscapes and archaeological evidence of long-standing Indigenous use and occupation more closely resembles what many people expect for a national park , it likely will receive some of the same public critique that the Gateway Arch and other national parks redesignated during the first Trump administration have received.
In rare cases, a community, group or other organization proposes adding an area that is not currently managed by the National Park Service to the system, but that process takes a lot of time .
It is more common to change the formal designation of a property already within the system, as has happened with this redesignation of Chiricahua.

Similarly, Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore became Indiana Dunes National Park in 2019. That same year, White Sands National Monument in New Mexico became White Sands National Park . And in 2020, New River Gorge National River in West Virginia became New River Gorge National Park and Preserve .

There are redesignation efforts underway seeking to make national parks in other locations as well, including the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area in New Jersey and Pennsylvania, Apostle Islands National Lakeshore in Wisconsin, and Rock Creek Park in the District of Columbia.
In my measure, it is simply a waiting game to see whether these National Park Service sites will also be redesignated to national parks.

Making Chiricahua a national park was a bipartisan effort – co-sponsored by Arizona U.S. Reps. Juan Ciscomani, a Republican, and Greg Stanton, a Democrat – that has received some opposition for several reasons.

The complaints have highlighted fears that the new label will bring increased tourism and overcrowding in what is considered a small park with limited infrastructure . Now that Chiricahua has been redesignated, the potential influx of new visitors in the coming years could affect the more personal and isolated experience that they currently appreciate.

However, the only real changes in these places would be in marketing – the signs, brochures and merchandise sold in gift shops. But these changes have an important effect: The tagline of “new national park” markets well to potential visitors .

But the funding that Chiricahua receives from the federal government will not change, and the label of “national park” won’t actually protect this landscape any better than it already is under the stewardship of the National Park Service.
This article includes material previously published in an article about the potential redesignation of Ocmulgee Mounds on Dec. 8, 2025.

articles.title: An AI model’s false tip to Philadelphia police reveals how digital agents can do as they’re told and still cause trouble
articles.author:
<name>Anat Lior, Assistant Professor of Law, Drexel University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/anat-lior-2494459"/>
paras: An anonymous tip arrived on PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a website run by the Philadelphia Police Department, on July 18, 2026.
“I may have information regarding this case,” it stated, and claimed the writer had seen someone matching the suspect’s description near the scene of a crime.
The tip was false. The page described no suspect, and the informer was, in fact, Claude Haiku 4.5, an AI model made by San Francisco-based Anthropic.

The tip was flagged as spam and never reached detectives. Anthropic found it in late September while reviewing its own test records. They alerted police on Oct. 8 and described the incident in a report they published Oct. 9. Philadelphia police disclosed it that day as well.

AI companies now build “ agents ,” versions of their chatbots that can operate a web browser, click buttons and fill in forms on a user’s behalf. To measure how well an agent does this, companies run it through thousands of practice tasks, often live on the internet.
According to Anthropic, the false tip was generated during a routine test of the model.

In this test, Haiku 4.5 was told to invent sample tasks on randomly chosen webpages and then carry them out. One of those pages happened to be about an unsolved Philadelphia homicide, and it had a tip form.
The model’s instructions listed things it must never do: Log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases and submit anything destructive.
So, the model wrote a plausible-sounding tip, left the optional name and contact boxes blank, and clicked submit.
Anthropic says the test records indicate the tip was generated as sample content for a practice task, not to mislead police.

The police tip was one of several incidents in Anthropic’s report. In another incident, a research model was supposed to practice on a copy of a government form. When the copy failed to load, it went to the real government website and submitted the form there. Other Claude models found ways around paywalls and access limits to reach data they needed.

Anthropic attributes these incidents to the persistence of its software. When the model can’t finish a task the way it was told, it finds a work-around instead of stopping to ask the human who gave it its initial task.

That habit comes partly from how these systems learn – much of their skill is built through trial and error. The model attempts a task many times and is rewarded when it succeeds. If the training accidentally rewards cutting corners, the model learns that cutting corners pays. Researchers call this “ reward hacking .” A human student drilled only on getting the right answer, by any means necessary, might learn the same lesson.

However, instructions given to an AI agent are never complete. A human worker who is told “Don’t buy anything or log in” would still know not to send police a made-up eyewitness account. But the model has no such common sense to fall back on. It treated a list of forbidden actions as the full boundary of acceptable behavior.

This is also why these models “ hallucinate ,” making things up. AI agents are built to produce fluent, plausible text. Asked to fill a tip form with an example, the model wrote what a tip typically sounds like, with no regard for the truthfulness of its content.
As a law professor who studies AI governance , two concerns stand out for me: scale and control.

The larger concern is scale. AI agents are moving out of the lab and into products people already use. Google’s Chrome browser now has a feature called auto browse that lets its Gemini assistant click through websites and fill in forms. Perplexity’s Comet browser and Anthropic’s Claude in Chrome extension do the same.

Every task a person hands to an agent is another chance for something to go wrong. If agents carry out a million tasks a day, a mistake that happens only once in 10,000 tasks would happen about 100 times a day. Those mistakes could mean false reports that take up police time, benefits or loan applications filed with wrong information, or payments and bookings the user never approved.

Anthropic itself notes that several incidents happened during ordinary use of Claude Haiku 4.5, not just testing. OpenAI has similarly reported its own agents reaching government sites in unplanned ways .

AI companies can’t fully control their agents, and that may lead to more harm and to gaps in who is held liable. These types of harms could include defamation , bias , deceit and social engineering and much more . It might seem fair not to hold a company responsible for actions it couldn’t control. But in cases like these, no other person or organization clearly controls the agent either, which could leave people who were harmed by the AI agent without anyone to hold legally responsible.

In my view, AI agents should be told what they may do, not just what they may not do, and anything AI companies send into the real world should be checked first. Until those safeguards are standard, any public online form, from a police tip line to a benefits application, could be receiving AI-written submissions that lack intuition and common sense. Their errors could, for example, deprive resources from real emergencies or deny benefits a person is entitled to . Meanwhile, victims of that harm may struggle to get compensation due to the lack of clarity around who had control over the AI agent.
Read more of our stories about Philadelphia and Pennsylvania , or sign up for our Philadelphia newsletter on Substack .
Anat Lior is affiliated with Yale, Drexel, WTW, and Relm.

articles.title: Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work
articles.author:
<name>Kenneth Greene, Professor of Government, The University of Texas at Austin</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/kenneth-greene-2768443"/>
paras: Politics is about the distribution of power and money. So it comes as little surprise that many politicians campaign on the material benefits that citizens can expect if those candidates win.

President Donald Trump has been no different in this respect. He has promised voters, among other things, a “ DOGE dividend ” using money saved by cutting federal jobs, rebates from tariff revenues , and a diversion of money currently used to subsidize health insurance companies directly to Americans.

But his pledge to give US$5,000 to every U.S. citizen if Republicans retain majorities in the House and Senate in the November 2026 midterm elections had a different dimension. This offer wasn’t a rebate for taxes paid or a subsidy for an impacted constituency. Instead, it was tied to an electoral outcome. That brings it closer to vote buying, which raises concerns from a legal point of view .

For this to actually happen, it needs congressional approval – and Republican legislators haven’t taken action. But Trump has yet to rescind the idea, which could cost over $1 trillion. So it’s time to ask whether it could make a difference in the midterms, where margins are tight in key races .

I’m a political scientist who has studied for the past decade vote buying in countries around the world. Cash for votes may seem like a straightforward way to win support, but my research shows that offering people money rarely changes their vote.

The practice dates back to ancient Rome and was a staple of American political machines from the 19th century to the mid-20th century in New York City, Chicago and states including Georgia, Missouri, New Jersey, Ohio and Virginia.

By diverting public money for partisan purposes, local power brokers cultivated relationships with particular constituencies, such as newly arrived immigrants . Institutional reforms, including the professionalization of government bureaucracies at the federal and local levels, slowly constricted these political machines until the last holdout in Chicago succumbed by the late 1970s.
But in recent decades, vote buying has surged in new democracies, with politicians in at least 73 countries offering cash, food, clothes, building supplies, medical care or legal advice for votes.

If vote buying is so common, it stands to reason that it must work. But a survey of recent research shows otherwise. On average, I have found that the vote-buying attempts across 10 countries and 57 elections around the world have had no detectable influence.

Why are the electoral returns so poor? For vote buying to work, the value of the benefits people receive has to outweigh the factors pushing them toward an opposing party. As in the U.S., voters around the world make their choices based on considerations such as their own partisanship; issue preferences; the performance of the incumbent party; the perceived competence of the candidates; and more. Very few voters in any electorate are truly indifferent .

As long as those factors together outweigh the value of the benefits that people would receive to switch, vote buying fails. And that’s what typically happens, as I explain in my new book, “ Against the Machine .”
There are three specific reasons why vote buying usually flops.

First, local competition creates vigorous campaigns that amp up partisan sentiments. These sentiments influence voters’ responses to electoral gifts. If you already like the political machine, you interpret its gifts as a sign that it cares about your welfare. But if you strongly identify with an opposing party – and therefore are a potential target of vote-buying efforts – you interpret gifts as an attempt to manipulate your vote and deprive you of basic political rights.

This calculation is one reason why vote-buying attempts can backfire, as a vivid example from Mexico shows. In 2018, two vote brokers working for Mexico’s conservative National Action Party were accosted by local voters in Nuevo Laredo. Angry residents stripped the brokers down to their underwear and painted them with the party’s blue color from head to toe, decorating them with the words “ Vote for the PAN for 500 pesos .”

The second reason vote buying often fails is that competitive elections make it difficult for party machines to identify the best voters to target. Strong opposition identifiers react negatively, but weakly opposed voters might trade their vote for a payday. The trouble is that even if local vote brokers can pinpoint these voters before the election, they’re also among the most susceptible to the influence of standard campaigning. That makes them moving targets : Their changing preferences mean that machines end up inadvertently paying voters who either don’t need gifts to vote for them or would need more to actually change their decision.

Finally, even when voters who are good targets get these benefits, they often look for an escape hatch to vote their sincere preferences anyway. The secret ballot provides one if they trust that it’s truly secret.

It turns out that people are acutely aware of who’s watching them vote. When they see poll watchers only from the party machine, they worry that their votes could be discovered by spies, cameras or by other means. But when they also see poll watchers from an opposing party, they believe that ballot secrecy is preserved and that they can vote sincerely without punishment.

Taken together, these reasons have led me to optimistically conclude that the effectiveness of vote buying depends not on the party machine’s prowess but on the strength of the parties that oppose it.
Vote buying has a checkered recent history in elections around the world, but could the “Trump dividend” swing the midterms? I see that scenario as unlikely.

Partisanship, a core element that makes people resistant to vote buying, is very strong in the U.S. electorate . There’s no need to pay committed Republicans, while committed Democrats will see the offer as a bald monetization of politics that can deepen their antagonism.
The design of Trump’s offer also makes it likely to flounder. Promising to pay everyone gets around the targeting challenge, but it also creates what social scientists call a “free-rider problem.”

At issue is that people tend to behave in selfish ways. If they expect a certain outcome anyway, they’ll make a decision based on self-interest. For example, independents and less committed Democrats who could be swayed by a $5,000 check might think they can avoid feeling like a sellout if they vote sincerely but they will still get paid as long as others switch their vote to Republican.

In theory, there is one way Trump’s offer could succeed. Research shows that buying turnout, rather than trying to change vote choices, is routinely effective . But all the examples come from countries where party officials actively monitor who comes to the polls. Without that surveillance, which is illegal in the U.S., the free-rider problem could bedevil turnout as well.

But whether enacted or not, the promise of cash for votes has a big downside for democracy. It means that no one will know whether victorious Republican candidates won this November because Americans preferred their policies and gave them a mandate – or because they expected to get paid.
Kenneth Greene's research has been funded by the National Science Foundation, the University of Texas at Austin, and the Mellon Foundation.

articles.title: El Niño is threatening California’s fragile coast again – the 1982-83 El Niño opened eyes to the serious erosion risks
articles.author:
<name>Gary Griggs, Distinguished Professor of Earth & Planetary Sciences, University of California, Santa Cruz</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/gary-griggs-168621"/>
paras: California’s coastal bluffs and beaches look rugged, but they can be surprisingly fragile in the face of a powerful El Niño.

The state saw that in 1982-83, when storms amid one of the most destructive El Niño winters in California history battered the coastline with powerful waves and torrential rain, leaving hundreds of millions of dollars in damage in its wake. The storms coincided with elevated sea levels, high astronomical tides and very large waves delivered by repeated storms.

Extreme waves that winter destroyed one-third of the Santa Monica Pier and tore off large sections of the Huntington Beach Pier and the Paradise Cove Pier, while also damaging the Seal Beach, San Clemente and Malibu piers. Numerous seawalls, decks and stairways were torn apart, and 33 oceanfront homes were destroyed.
Massive waves also stripped millions of cubic yards of sand from Southern California beaches, and sections of the Pacific Coast Highway suffered severe flooding, mudslides and washouts.

Along the central coast, waves and high-tide flooding eroded bluffs . In Pacifica, just outside San Francisco, the edge of a sandy cliff lost over 65 feet as it failed, collapsing onto the beach and forcing the relocation of a two-story building and removal of an entire row of mobile homes. This area of high but weak bluffs continued to erode over the subsequent decades, forcing the demolition of bluff-top homes and apartments.

The El Niño now building in 2026-27 is forecast to be even stronger , and coastal homes are already seeing damage . I have studied coastal geology and oceanography in California for nearly six decades. With the conditions expected this year, coastal flooding, coastal erosion and landslides are likely, and more dramatic cliff collapses wouldn’t be a surprise, though every El Niño is different.

El Niño is one end of a climate pattern that swings from warm to cold every few years and can change weather patterns around the world. Normally dry areas can experience flooding rains, and wet areas can suffer droughts. The U.S. Pacific Coast in particular can take a beating from powerful atmospheric river storms with heavy downpours.

El Niños begin with a shift in wind patterns, which normally push warm waters from east to west along the equator. For reasons still not fully understood, the trade winds die and the warm pool of water in the western Pacific begins to flow back toward the coast of South America.
Part of this warm mass moves north toward the coast of California as a pulse or bulge, known as a Kelvin wave, and it begins to have far-ranging impacts.

Seawater expands as it warms, which raises sea level along the Pacific Coast for weeks during these periodic events. While all El Niños are not created equal, during the very large 1982-83 event, sea levels were elevated above predicted high tides by about a foot in San Diego to nearly 2 feet in San Francisco .
These higher sea levels can reach higher elevations and last longer.

The elevated sea levels also allow storm waves to break closer to the shoreline, eroding beaches and bluffs , leading to damage and destruction of both private oceanfront development and public infrastructure, including streets and highways, bridges and piers, and parks and recreational facilities.
Much of California’s coastal and shoreline development took place from the late 1940s to the late 1970s when the state’s population exploded.
Homes were built on beaches, bluffs and dunes during a period when the coastal storm climate was generally mild and there were no real concerns with coastal hazards and future sea-level rise.
This changed quickly in 1978 when the first strong El Niño in recent memory arrived, raising alarm about the hazards ocean development was exposed to.

The extreme 1982-83 El Niño that followed a few years later caused about US$328 million (in 2025 dollars) in damage to oceanfront property, $87 million in losses to recreational facilities such as piers, parking lots and access stairs, and $66 million in damage to large engineering structures such as breakwaters and jetties designed to protect harbors from storm waves.

At least in the short term, the 1982-83 El Niño winter changed popular perceptions of the stability or security of oceanfront homes and other shoreline development. Building restrictions were tightened, insurance rates rose, and many requests for new seawall permits were submitted.
But then it was back to business as usual, as new arrivals to the coast outbid each other for the same oceanfront homes damaged a few years before.

Increased coastal armoring , such as seawalls and rock revetments , helped limit erosion during other very large El Niños that followed, in 1997-98 and 2015-16 , along with lucky timing that large waves arrived at low points in the monthly tidal cycle, leading to significantly less property damage than in 1982-83 .

The coast was not so fortunate in winter 2022-23 , when high seas and waves alone caused an estimated $4.7 billion in economic losses along California’s coast. The simultaneous occurrence of large storm waves, high tides and elevated sea levels were almost identical to the El Niño conditions in early 1983, 40 years earlier.
The state’s latest climate assessment , released Oct. 19, 2026, warns of more intense storms and increased erosion as temperatures increase and sea level continues to rise.

The southern end of the state is already suffering wave damage from an exceptionally busy Pacific hurricane season , also fueled by El Niño. Swells have stripped away beaches and destroyed homes near San Diego . The state’s storm season, when powerful atmospheric rivers bring downpours, typically begins in October or November and runs through early spring.
The magnitude of the emerging 2026-27 El Niño , likely to be one of the strongest on record, is making clear that coastal communities need to adapt now to a very different future.
How each coastal neighborhood, city and county responds will vary depending upon their local conditions and vulnerability to coastal erosion and flooding.

While many communities are stockpiling sandbags, clearing culverts and preparing evacuation plans, there are limits on what they can do to stop erosion . Building seawalls and rock revetments can provide some protection if well designed, but they can also create new problems , including leading to the loss of beaches over time as sea levels continue to rise. Putting more sand on beaches is costly and very short-lived.

Extensive shoreline development, eroding bluffs, aging infrastructure and increasing exposure to extreme weather are placing growing pressure on coastal communities and shorelines around the world. Some will eventually face the difficult transition from continued shoreline protection to retreating from the coast – either planned retreat or following repeated damage.

There is little that any developed coastal area can do at this point to minimize the impacts of the El Niño underway. What they can do is prepare to manage the risks and try to adapt to the changing future .

articles.title: Changing the Zoning for most of Seattle
articles.author: Ross Bleakney
paras: “ Neighborhood Residential ” (previously called “Single-Family”) is the most common zoning type in Seattle. It makes up about 2/3 of the land zoned for development in the city. This is where we have the greatest potential for improving population density and affordability in Seattle. Here is a proposal for simple changes that could make a huge difference. This zoning type used to be three minimum lot sizes. Now there’s only one: 5,000 square feet . Along with lowering the size limit for new lots, other rules are now a bit more liberal. While these changes are laudable, they are still complicated and aren’t as liberal as what Spokane has . I believe we can do better.

We should get rid of minimum lot sizes in the city. As long as a builder adheres to other regulations they should be free to build small-lot homes, like row houses or skinny houses . Some people will still want bigger lots. But it is quite likely this would give a lot more people the opportunity to own both a home and the land under it.

The city restricts both the size of the lots, the dimensions of the structure, and the number of units. This is labeled “ Maximum Density ” in the code. We should eliminate these limits. Rules and regulations should be based on the structure itself, not how many people can live there. I can understand why people don’t want to see a big building next to them. But if you can build a three-story house next to me, I don’t care how many units it has. It might as well be a short apartment or condo. This would also allow for a lot more houses to be converted to apartments. Limit the dimensions of the structure, not the number of units.

There are also rules about “ lot coverage ” or what portion of the land can be covered by the structure. Typically this limits the structure to using half the lot. These rules are designed in part to limit water runoff. But the structure should simply be considered as part of the rules governing impervious surfaces . A house taking up 60% of the lot is basically the same as a house taking up 30% and parking taking up 30%. As long as the developer adheres to the stormwater code, both should be allowed.

Parking requirements push up the cost of new construction. As a result, this pushes up the cost of buying a new place or renting a new unit. But since new units impact the cost of existing units, all renters are hurt by the parking requirement. In contrast, existing owners aren’t effected by the regulations since they already own their property. Additional parking in a neighborhood can be considered a benefit to everyone who lives in the neighborhood (which is why the requirement was enacted in the first place). People who live there or visit are less likely to park on the street. But since existing owners pay nothing for this benefit, the burden falls entirely on those who rent or are looking to buy. If you believe that parking is a public good (and I don’t) then everyone should chip in for public parking lots. Regardless, we should remove all parking requirements for new housing.

Floor Area Ratio or FAR is the ratio of a building’s total floor area to the size of the piece of land upon which it is built. A FAR of 1.0 means that you can cover the entire lot area with a building that is one story high. It also means that you can cover half the lot with a two-story building (or a third of the lot with three-story building, etc.). A ratio of 0.5 means that you can only cover half the lot with a one-story building (or one quarter of the lot with a two-story building). Likewise, a ratio or 2.0 means that you can cover the entire lot with a building that is two stories high (or half the lot with a four-story building, etc.).

The land zoned neighborhood residential is limited to three stories. Thus any FAR less than 3.0 limits construction. While the FAR limit specified by the city for neighborhood residential varies quite a bit depending on various factors, it is always less than 3.0. This limits the amount of housing that can be built. FAR regulations should be eliminated for this zoning type (if not others).

A “setback” is the minimum distance which a building or other structure must be set back from the property line. There are rules that apply to the front, rear and each side. The front setback is typically based on aesthetics, which are debatable. Paris has no setbacks. Montreal has small setbacks. These are widely considered extremely attractive cities.

Other setbacks are based on the interests of immediate neighbors. In a lot of cases, people don’t want the new owner to build right up to the property line. But side setbacks and rear setbacks should be negotiable. The neighbors — the only people who would actually be impacted by development in those areas — should be able to allow it. Just as you can buy “air rights” over a property, the neighbor should be able to sell development rights right up to the edge of property. There are plenty of people — whose house is already in the middle of the lot — that wouldn’t mind such development at all. Just as importantly, this would also row houses — with the houses right next to each other — in any subdivision.

These changes are relatively simple. They would not alter the height limits that exist. Yet they would change the rules that govern the vast majority of land that can be developed in the city. A lot more people would be able to afford to live in Seattle.

articles.title: State Lawmaker, SDOT Director Clash Over Aurora Avenue Overhaul
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Slow progress in advancing plans for the future of Aurora Avenue appears to be leading to mounting tensions between state legislators and the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). Those tensions came to a head in an email exchange just this month between Representative Julia Reed (D-36th LD, Queen Anne) and Acting SDOT Director Angela Brady, a copy of which was obtained by The Urbanist.

The spicy exchange comes more than four years after state lawmakers set aside $50 million for improvements to Seattle's deadliest roadway, which also operates as State Route 99 for its entire length within city limits. An earmark spearheaded by former state Senator Reuven Carlyle, who referred to Aurora as a "scar, ripping through the center of our city", those funds were intended to be a down payment on a fully transformed corridor that he compared to the Champs-Élysées.

But things remain stuck in the planning stage, despite legislative direction in 2022 targeting upgrades between N 90th Street and N 105th Street as a demonstration project that would pave the way for changes elsewhere. SDOT ultimately did not follow that direction, setting up a safety project to look at the entire corridor between South Lake Union and N 145th Street and looping in King County Metro and Seattle Public Utilities in a move that was certain to make the project harder to implement.

Meanwhile, transportation advocates have shifted their focus further south, to the stretch of Aurora Avenue that divides sections of the Fremont neighborhood from each other. Reconnect Fremont, a project of the Aurora Reimagined Coalition (ARC), represents a push for new marked crossings and bus stops that will start to stitch the neighborhood back together. Families with kids at B.F. Day Elementary School who live on the east side of Aurora currently have to use an overpass at N 41st Street to access school, something that doesn't really work for households who get around by bike.
"We want to cut through the endless studies and build momentum through action," ARC stated in a blog post on Reconnecting Fremont earlier this year.

That goal appears to be shared by Rep. Reed, who serves as Vice Chair of the House transportation committee. Following up on an August call that took place with SDOT and staff from Mayor Katie Wilson's office, Rep. Reed wrote to SDOT Director Brady on October 2 – more than a month after that call took place.

"Wanted to check in from our call in August about looking for the City to take action on the highly needed demonstration projects connecting Fremont across Aurora," Reed wrote. She referenced a commitment made during the calll to set up a meeting between ARC and the consultant team currently looking at potential upgrades to Aurora, from the firm Parametrix. "[I]n our call, the Mayor’s office committed to looking at these projects and taking more urgent action to implement them or at least coming up with a plan in the short term – has that happened?"

Brady's response skirted around the issue of near-term improvements along Aurora in Fremont, instead reiterating the work the SDOT already has done to improve safety on the corridor without directly utilizing state funding.

"We share the sense of urgency that Aurora Ave N is in need of improvements now," Brady wrote. "Over the last three years, we have expanded bus lane operations, installed No Turn on Red and Leading Pedestrian Intervals (LPIs), repainted and widened all crosswalks, added center medians and hardened centerlines to reduce turning conflicts, and updated signal timing corridor-wide to increase pedestrian crossing times. We are currently wrapping up construction of a new signal at N 137 th St and completing designs for another package of additional near-term improvements."

But Brady, who took over as Interim SDOT Director in January after a long stint in the city's Office of the Waterfront & Civic Projects, also told Reed that the department has been having a hard time figuring out how to use the $50 million in funding from the 2022 Move Ahead Washington (MAW) transportation package.

"Generally, we have found that the MAW funds have not been easy for SDOT to use for near-term work. They are administered by WSDOT Local Programs similar to a state grant, making them challenging for the City to pivot and use quickly," Brady said. "Seattle is currently exploring various scenarios for sequencing MAW dollars – including near term improvements and a more focused, targeted approach to longer-term improvements. We look forward to discussing those options with you ahead of session."

Reed wrote back visibly frustrated, framing Brady as backing off a promise to set up the direct meeting between ARC and Parametrix, and a commitment to provide concrete next steps on quick build projects that could help to reconnect Fremont.

"I’m sure it is not the city’s intention to go back on its word to a sitting representative and member of the Transportation committee — especially since as we discussed the heart of this problem is a lack of trust in SDOT to administer the state funds effectively," Reed wrote. "I’ve worked in city government a long time so I speak roundabout email as well as anyone. Please do not spray water on my inbox and then try to convince me it is raining."

Reed was even more blunt in an aside in a follow-up email directed to Alex Hudson, at the time Katie Wilson's Senior Policy Advisor on Transportation & Livability. (Hudson has since spent several weeks filling in as Wilson's Interim Press Secretary, but is now returning to her prior role.)

"If the city does not plan to keep the commitments we discussed then I will note that 1) the City is not a trustworthy partner than can be relied on to do what it says it will do when it comes to Transportation work, which will just for the record have an influence on the level of effort I want to put in to advocate for city priorities at the state level and 2) recommend to Chair Fey that the $50 million could be better used in a more directed fashion to improve near term conditions on Aurora," Reed wrote.

Reed, responding to an inquiry about the email exchange via text, made it clear that funding for Aurora remains a priority for her office, but reiterated her frustration with the City of Seattle's pace of action.

"I will say for the record I have no wish to diminish funding for Aurora or to endanger the set aside which goes back to Reuven Carlyle days. But I do want SDOT to take ARC seriously and to take me seriously when I say that waiting two more years before you even think about doing a project is not acceptable," Reed wrote. "This is about trust as much as anything, and following through on the small commitments and pushing forward the bigger demonstration projects is how SDOT builds trust with me and the community that we’re really on the same page."

"Also I commend all the hard work ARC members have put in as volunteers to create a reasonable, achievable, and practical vision," Reed continued. "I don’t think they’re asking for that much and I think city departments should be doing cartwheels of joy to have community members who are so organically engaged at a time when SDOT routinely spends thousands trying to produce even a fraction of this engagement."

Since the email exchange, Reed and Brady met one-on-one this past Friday, a meeting that reportedly went positively. SDOT spokesperson Ethan Bergerson portrayed the department as making progress on Aurora in a statement provided to The Urbanist in the wake of that meeting.

"Acting Director Angela Brady and SDOT staff have a commitment, responsibility, and desire to improve safety on Aurora Ave N. We greatly value Representative Reed’s partnership on this important project and appreciate the work of advocates in continuing to elevate and participate in solutions for the critical needs on Aurora Ave N," Bergerson wrote. "There was a misunderstanding about a commitment made in a meeting regarding the Aurora Ave Project. Now that we’re aware of the misunderstanding, we are scheduling a meeting in November between members of the Aurora Reimagined Coalition and our consultant team."

Bergerson noted that SDOT is working toward wrapping up the planning phase on the Aurora project by next year, a condition of state grant funding the city has already received. $3 million allocated by the legislature remains unobligated, out of the city's reach. Receiving the remaining $44 million will require direct coordination with legislators.

Whether the Aurora project can finally see some forward momentum remains to be seen. And Reed's email exchange voiced concerns that many transportation advocates have raised around the slow pace of work to tackle some of Seattle's most dangerous streets, with the goings-on inside the city's insular transportation department seemingly impenetrable even to a state legislator. Though Mayor Katie Wilson issued an executive order in August directing SDOT to accelerate work on Vision Zero projects, many of the highest-profile corridor overhauls included in the 2024 Seattle Transportation Levy remain in early stages.

"Aurora Avenue is Seattle's most dangerous street. It is polluted, noisy, and divides our neighborhoods. Representative Reed is a strong and steadfast supporter of ARC and our mission to change Aurora for the better. She has worked tirelessly alongside her constituents to ensure SDOT's plan for Aurora is truly transformational," Aurora Reimagined Coalition member Carlo Alcantara told The Urbanist . "Like Rep Reed, ARC would like to see more near-term action on demonstration projects like Reconnect Fremont. These demonstration projects start to reimagine Aurora as a neighborhood main street rather than a highway bisecting our neighborhoods."

articles.title: Housing Accountability Act Puts Tiny Beaux Arts Village in the Spotlight
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Changes to state law intended to broaden access to more affordable types of housing are reverberating in some unexpected places, including within Puget Sound's smallest jurisdictions. Last week, the town council in Beaux Arts Village – population 310 – met to approve a slate of temporary zoning changes, under threat of state sanctions and prompted by the 2025 Housing Accountability Act. While the vote was unanimous, the meeting included plenty of hand-wringing about the path the town had taken to get to that point.

Clocking in at just 0.17 square miles, Beaux Arts Village is a town entirely ensconced within the City of Bellevue, a pocket of narrow, tree-lined streets where golf carts are more commonplace than apartment buildings. Founded in 1908 as an artist's colony, the town's initial boosters drew residents with advertisements in the Seattle Times touting the fledgling community as "an expedition into the realms of Utopia." The town's primary amenity is a 1,100 foot stretch of beach, which only town property owners have access to as members of a separate, non-profit organization known as the Western Academy of Beaux Arts.

In 1954, Beaux Arts officially incorporated, to "protect the beach and the Village lifestyle," according to the town's website today. It had taken two years for Beaux Arts to reach the required 300-resident minimum necessary to be able to become a town, but just over seven decades later the population has only changed by six residents. Today, the median home value in Beaux Arts Village is $2.6 million.

In the decades since the implementation of Washington's 1990 Growth Management Act (GMA), the state-mandated growth plans in enclaves like Beaux Arts Village haven't traditionally been subjected to much scrutiny. But in 2025, the state legislature passed the Housing Accountability Act , empowering the Washington Department of Commerce to directly evaluate whether local jurisdictions are meeting the expectations laid out in state law when it comes to accommodating housing. Before that law was approved, the only avenue for a local Comprehensive Plan to be found inadequate was through a citizen appeal – though the state has sometimes taken the drastic step of making that appeal itself in extreme circumstances.

In January, Commerce announced that Beaux Arts Village had been selected as one of the first eight jurisdictions ever subjected to "selected review" under the Housing Accountability Act. As part of that review, agency staff have been tasked with determining whether all eight are in compliance with all aspects of the GMA, including new provisions that direct localities to plan for housing across different income levels – requirements that many cities have found vexing.

Beaux Arts' 2024 Comprehensive Plan was reviewed with a fine-toothed comb, and in June a preliminary report was issued to town officials that listed everything that needed to be adjusted to get into alignment with state law, in Commerce's view. That letter gave town officials their marching orders, and started the clock.

"We've been at it for nine months. We presented a Comp Plan that I think is in alignment with what everybody here will believe is keeping with what the village is, which has been much like the past three or four Comp Plans that we put together," Beaux Arts Councilmember Tom Stowe said Tuesday. "Commerce came in and shredded it, basically, and said that we couldn't do what we basically wanted."

Beaux Arts Village's share of Puget Sound's expected housing growth over the coming decades is not substantial. In fact, when King County handed out housing growth targets across all 39 cities and towns countywide in 2021 – an expectation of the number of new units to plan for through 2044 – the number was just one. Its neighbor Bellevue is planning for 35,000.

And yet the town's existing land use, intended to preserve a "tranquil, calm living environment" per the current Beaux Arts Village Comprehensive Plan, has presented certain challenges when it comes to growth plan compliance. Per a 2021 adjustment to the GMA known as House Bill 1220, Beaux Arts Village is required to plan for that one housing unit to be occupied by a household making 30% of King County's median area income or below – households that overall have the greatest difficulty finding housing.

30% of King County's median income is just under $40,000 for a family of two, and residents bringing in that little income cannot afford the single family homes that make up the vast majority of the town's housing stock, nor can they afford the backyard cottages that are allowed on those lots either.

To make it feasible to build at least one home that could be within reach to that future low-income household, Commerce recommended that Beaux Arts Village officials adjust zoning to allow some type of multifamily housing within their borders. Beaux Arts ultimately settled on the idea of creating a co-living "overlay." Co-living housing, also referred to as single-room occupancy (SRO) homes, provide the lowest rents even when built without any subsidy.

Though the idea of allowing six units of co-living housing just on one block of Beaux Arts Village was considered by the town planning commission, but counting on six property owners to build that specific type of housing would likely fall short of providing the necessary capacity. Instead, a proposal advanced that would allow co-living housing outside of the town's "erosion control hazard area" closest to Lake Washington.

The Beaux Arts Village planning commission deadlocked 2-2 on the idea of scaling back Commerce's recommendation to allow six co-living units on all lots in the overlay, but the town council ultimately did scale that number back to four. The fewer units allowed in the overlay, the less likely that it is that any actual co-living projects will get built – an outcome that did come up Tuesday.
"If we think this is about somebody coming in and building, nobody is going to build this," Councilmember Stacy Saal said.

As a town of its size, there is no Beaux Arts Village town hall – just a town mailbox. Town council meetings take place in a rotating councilmember's home, which is how a dining room and adjoining kitchen was transformed into a public meeting room last week for the monthly town council. Twenty to thirty Beaux Arts residents packed into the space, standing in the hallway or sitting on the floor as their elected representatives debated town matters, including whether to get in compliance with state housing law.

The big incentive for councilmembers to act and adopt the interim ordinance, which will expire February 4, was the stick included in the Housing Accountability Act. In addition to being disqualified for some state grants, cities and towns deemed to be out of compliance with the GMA trigger what is known as the Builder's Remedy .

A brand new provision in state law, the Builder's Remedy requires the approval of any complete building permit – no matter whether the underlying project conflicts with the underlying zoning for the site, as long as certain requirements for on-site affordable units are met. Theoretically, this could lead to a ten story apartment building in Beaux Arts Village, as long as a subset of the new units are kept within certain rents.

"If we don't do this tonight, as you all remember, the consequence is we go out of compliance, and the low income builder remedy kicks in, and any low income builder comes in and can submit plans that totally ignore our zoning code, they can come in and build whatever they want," Beaux Arts Mayor Aletha Howes the crowd in attendance on Tuesday. "The only thing they have to follow is setbacks and tree code. Everything else is blown out of water."

So far no jurisdiction has actually triggered the Builder's Remedy, with Carnation getting fully into compliance earlier this summer, and Bainbridge Island going the same route as Beaux Arts and approving a temporary ordinance a few days after Carnation. But in Beaux Arts just as there was on Bainbridge Island, some voices pushed for a more oppositional stance against state review.
During Tuesday's public hearing, local resident Dan Bridges urged councilmembers to take a more adversarial position.

"Well-meaning councils and boards sometimes lose sight of the fact that public agencies, state agencies – who we trust, like our parents, right? – they're still political agencies, and they have an agenda and they have a point of view. That point of view is not always the correct point of view," Bridges said. "Having an outside [entity] of coming to advocate for us would be helpful. And I would suggest if you haven't done that yet, you might consider doing that and not simply accept what some state agency is telling you. Only a judge is the one who decides the law."
For now at least, Beaux Arts Village has deemed the path of least resistance to be compliance.

"It is not that we are not receptive of what we're hearing," Stowe told public commenters. "It's that we quite frankly are up against them to comply, or they're going to go over us and say you have no authority and allow whatever zoning or buildings they say under the code – under Commerce's interpretation of the code, which has not necessarily been ours – and we have pointed that out that we don't read the law the same way they do."
As one of the first jurisdictions being put under the Housing Accountability Act microscope, Beaux Arts officials expressed clear frustration at the process of state review over the past few months.

They're not alone in that frustration. When members of the Carnation City Council held a public hearing with the Department of Commerce in July, many of the same concerns raised in Beaux Arts surfaced – about staff time, not an insignificant issue for a small city or town, and confusion over the purpose of the new law.

"Is this supposed to be helpful for us?," Carnation deputy Mayor Jessica Merizan asked Commerce staff at that July 9 meeting. "Because it really seems like you've pulled a lot of staff time, and the point seems to be saving staff time because these types of errors are happening. It just kind of feels like this is a teacher double-checking work, and not necessarily, these are areas of the community, in the region that perhaps need support, and we're here to offer that."

In Beaux Arts Village, Howes directly referred to what the Commerce department had been tasked with doing as "overreach" and called the idea of the state forcing local officials to spend scarce staff time on that review as an "unfunded mandate" that she called "bullshit."

"I am still pursuing the legislative changes in the next session with [Representative] Zahn, [Representative Thai], and [the Association of Washington Cities] is still pushing the seven legal arguments that we brought to them, and the seven other cities are also pushing to get those changes," Howes said, noting the temporary ordinance's four-month duration. "So if something moves during that time frame, then we can amend. If something doesn't move and it goes to final...you know, we'll see how the legislative session goes in '27."

Meanwhile, five additional cities and towns – including Woodway, Darrington, Gold Bar, Brier, and DuPont – are still in the process of coming into compliance, work that was spurred on by the Housing Accountability Act. And then next year, a whole new slate of jurisdictions will be announced.

articles.title: Sunday Movie: Service-Led Planning in California Rail
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: In 2004 California released an excellent service-led plan to expand its state rail network, both the high-speed rail projects and other corridors and a few BRT connectors. This video by nandert goes in-depth on why service-led planning is an important paradigm all agencies should use (5:33), the benefits of California’s plan, and how the governing boards would need major structural changes and reforming their priorities to actually make it happen this well.

He defines service-led planning as “Start by determining where the transit demand and need is, and tailor the plan to meet that demand.” In other words, determining how much of what kind of service each corridor needs. Then draw up cost estimates for the resulting lines to operators (agencies). The California plan specifies the rail/bus mode and frequency, but you could also leave the mode for a later step before assigning them to agencies, as Jarrett Walker does.

The difference between this and most transit planning is, corridors are chosen to meet the bulk of mobility/trip needs, without certain city/county jurisdictions having undue influence to override these for demands that contradict them. It also puts frequency first in the spec rather than leaving is as an afterthought, so the public can see what minimum frequency the entire network or each project will have so that they can see what their experience will be like.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The 38 Best Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. Every place on the list has been open for at least six months, proving its merit.

Like many menus, this map updates every quarter — removal from the Eater 38 doesn’t mean a restaurant isn’t still awesome and won’t return in the future. New to the map as of August 2026: unassuming neighborhood gem Three Sacks Full; seafood-focused French bistro L’Oursin; and La Cabaña, where you can find some of the city’s best pupusas.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
In July 2026, we updated this map to include tapas bar Ocho, choose-your-own-beefy-adventure steakhouse Asadero Prime, and neighborhood Thai mainstay Pestle Rock.
